text_translated_detailed:
Batavia. To the Honorable Lord Joan Maatzuijcker, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords of the Council of India. Amboina. A missive from the Honorable Governor and the Council there, addressed to Your Honors, dated the 5th of May 1668.

Your Honors, Most Esteemed, Highly Respected, Valiant and Wise Gentlemen, and Generous Lords, High Commanding Gentlemen,

In this current year, God be praised, with the safe passage of the fleet ships Pegu and Witte Leeuw, as well as the Yacht Meliskerken, all via Makassar, have arrived safely with us. Your Honors' pleasant letters, with their attachments, dated the 11th of January and 23rd of February, together with the Cargoes for this province that were loaded therein, according to the respective invoices, for which liberal provision—especially now that the long delay of the fatherland's ships at the Cape and the shortage of provisions has caused much scarcity—we believe we have sufficient reason to thank Your Honors, which we do hereby, wishing that it had pleased God that in return a more ample supply had been able to come to Your Honors for the relief of the Company's heavy burdens, as unfortunately it has not, the harvest also coming so late that we have had to hold back the fleet ship Klaverskerken for somewhat longer than our desire would have been, in order to fulfill Your Honors' and the Esteemed Superintendent's orders, had we wished to send it away empty. But considering that Your Honors desire both the cloves and the fleet ship speedily, nothing else can be done but to perform all due diligence and to take patience further. The hooker-boat the Pimpelmees, sent by Your Honors to the fleet on the 9th of January, with letters and the loaded Cargo (as the chief officers say) was indeed in sight of the castles at Makassar, but nevertheless no word was heard there of our ships or flags, whereupon it proceeded via Buton and arrived here safely on the 19th of February. The thoughts at that time were that the Esteemed Superintendent with the force must have been at Bima, to conclude there the end of the glorious successes. However, the following boats and letters from His Excellency soon revealed to us that we had been mistaken, the ships having lain at anchor behind the island before the Company's Castle Rotterdam. Also, the scruple, given the lack of knowledge in Amboina on the 5th of May 1668 of the success, would not have made them bold enough to come closer and to see properly. Yet the delay does not appear to be great from his aforementioned letters, since he finds himself sufficiently provisioned with everything, and has moreover provided us with various provisions, ammunition, etc., per Vlieland and Klaverskerken, to the amount of ƒ 23,173:—:2:, these boats having been sent there on the 30th of January and early March, and arrived here on the 22nd of February and 14th of March respectively, in good condition.

Regarding the last shipment, according to Your Honors' orders, the fleet ship Witte Leeuw is being held back, which in the meantime is still serving God's work on the fortifications, and the Meliskerken will, as soon as it is loaded with 7 barrels of gunpowder and some timber, if the same can be loaded therein (given the lack of a cargo hatch), also depart shortly for Makassar, as well as the Vlieland, if we find that it is not capable of rendering any particular service due to its great leakiness, which would be worthy of the delay. But it is very apparent that the aforementioned hooker will have to remain for the last shipment, and perhaps even over the year, to serve as an advisor in all circumstances, since the misfortune, to our sorrow, has befallen us that the small Yacht Boero, anchored on the same island on the north side at the place Sieko Mourassa and lying in the loading of planks, was wrecked on the 19th of February last by an unexpected northerly wind. The Provincial Captain named Evert Caspersz. of Amsterdam was brought to trial over this, which trial is still continuing. Otherwise, nothing can be said regarding the life and conduct of the aforementioned person. Meanwhile, this loss has deprived us of much convenience. We therefore hope that if the aforementioned hooker, as stated, were deemed necessary to remain here, we would not be doing wrong thereby.

To this end, a multitude of young trees are to be planted for the first time. At the visitation for the observation of the previously ordered plantation, as much as possible the hand is being held, according to our instruction set thereon, to be seen by resolution of the 30th of January, not doubting that the feared negligence will thereby be prevented. Amboina, the 5th of May 1668. This extraordinary visitation will take a long and tedious time before it is completed everywhere, since the visitors must examine all the trees, both small and large, and judge and report on their condition, with the taking of an oath that everything has been found as it should be. To this end are qualified the Ensign Jacques Compagon together with a sergeant with their assistants, and Your Honors will see the effect thereof in due time. Meanwhile, we note that some have been more concerned with maintaining their assigned number in the third [uncertain: possibly a measurement or administrative division], than with attending to the success, since many are set so close together that they deprive each other of nourishment. And for this reason it will be necessary with particular care to order the required distance noted in the aforementioned instruction. But here lies yet another matter that is tied up, which seems to have caused concern, for the successive orders also bring with them that each household must maintain 80 plants. Meanwhile, some throw away [uncertain: possibly "abandon" or "neglect"] for the lack of land to find the necessary space. If, however, this proposal should have the desired effect, as it should, and as is confirmed by the visitors, then it will be necessary to deviate from the order as much as is proper. This perhaps will cause no small offense to others where the matter does not lie thus, since what is new is often heard—the sluggishness of the Islanders toward clove cultivation, claiming that scarcely anyone finds themselves capable, with their own people, of harvesting their cloves with a good crop, but must invite their friends and hire other households to do so, at such great cost of entertainment, etc., that the owner in the end has little left over, and gives them little encouragement for that work. Amkorinc I M. Bar. Amboina on the 5th of May 1668. Concerning the outcome of affairs at Makassar, our aforementioned Esteemed Lord Cornelis Speelman, Superintendent Admiral, War Commander, etc., has sent us word speedily by missive dated the 5th of December by the Chialoup Timor, which arrived here on the 22nd of the same month. Over which lordly victory, just as we have steadily prayed to the great God thereto, so His Majesty has been brought the solemn thanksgiving with joy over this great salvation, whereby the state of the Esteemed Company under Your Excellency's wise governance, through the means of the untiring diligence of the aforementioned lord, remains blessed. Therefore we then take the liberty to wish Your Excellency with this Conquest much luck and the Most High's

text_translated_detailed: What has transpired on Ceram, insofar as it is known to us. — We now turn to the receivers of cloves, which Your Excellency and the Esteemed Superintendent's order has presented for just weighing, and the Inlander finds himself at least completely satisfied therewith, and the fiscal here shall also take good regard of this, as well as against private trading and purchasing of cloves, as is his duty, and to which Your Excellency is pleased to leave him, just as we cannot yet report that the new distribution of clove shells has caused any discontent. — Concerning the description of the heels, nothing can be remarked either — why the same should be deferred, since the first beginning is always the worst, for by continuing therewith, they fall into habit, and it becomes gradually lighter and clearer. The Papuans become ever more strange to us, which is proof that the Contract made by the Esteemed Superintendent with the Fidor Company produces good results, as we further learn from the letters of the Mister President in Ternate, the inclination and earnest Amboina, the 5th of May 1668 efforts of His Highness toward the prevention of these robbers, the only thing that has come to us from the same is their committed robbery on Tamboco, where they captured some 50 people and carried them away as booty. — When this was advised to the aforementioned Esteemed President on the 20th of December, we received on the 11th of February a reply, how His Highness had always given him knowledge — that those fellows had been out before the closing of the contract. — Meanwhile the Company made good on its promises of efforts, so that no more complaints could be heard, and besides delivering seven stolen boat-anchors, the Raja of Tamboco, as is told, wished to ask the Mister Superintendent for revenge over the loss of his people.

text_translated_detailed: Batavia. To the Esteemed Lord Joan Maatzuijker, Governor General. Esteemed, earnest, highly honored, manly, wise, and before the Esteemed Lords Councilors of India, and most generous lords. Your Esteemed, highly commanding lords. Our sole missive to you, dated the 5th of May, departed by the fluyt Klaverskerken, with instructions to the authorities to approach the bay of Bantheijn, and there to receive further orders from the Esteemed Lord Superintendent Admiral and Free Commander Cornelis Speelman. The same vessel was loaded with no more than 102,833 pounds of clove nails, which, God willing, Your Esteemed Lordship will have received by now. Since its departure from here, on the same day the yacht Meliskerke sailed to Macassar, carrying for Batavia 1,500 bundles of Ternate and Amboinese fuse, with 200 barrels of spoiled gunpowder. On the same day the small fluyt Breuckelen sailed to Timor. On the 30th of the same month, the Hilversum sailed to Macassar, which latter vessel, on the 19th of that same month, departed from Ternate in the roadstead, near Larique, having arrived with all that was salvageable in terms of timber and people, and there received the necessary provisions, without our being able to find it suitable to keep this vessel here and employ it in fetching stone for the works. Since Vlieland (being somewhat damaged) was still deemed suitable for that purpose, which was indeed done effectively. Meanwhile, on the 27th of June, the hooker-boat the Quickstart appeared here, coming from Macassar via Banda with letters sent by the Esteemed Lord Superintendent to this province, together with one from the Esteemed Lord Governor Jacob Cops, containing the unpleasant news of the Macassarese's new rebellion, brought about by the evil machinations of Train Crourou, set in motion, although by God's providence and careful investigation of the aforementioned lord, it came to light in good time. As Your Esteemed Lordship will have learned long ago from the fortunate voyage of the yacht the Cinnamon Tree.

text_translated_detailed: Now, sir, regarding Feldoet on Tidore, Bonoa—however, we do not yet have great reason to complain about this on behalf of the Dutch, except that the Reverend Predicant Simon de Buck recently was afflicted again with severe gout and lameness in his hands, without any appearance of speedy recovery. Upon his repeated request and having obtained permission from the Reverend Church Council here, he has been allowed by the Yacht Vlieland to proceed to Macassar and thereafter to procure consent to go to Batavia, where he impressed upon us that through change of air as well as better medicines and physicians or healers, he could be helped sooner and more completely. However, we would not have presumed to do this without your Excellency's or the Reverend Superintendent's permission, unless it were judged that the church would have no service from his Excellency to expect within five or six months, and for this reason we took comfort, trusting that in this matter we would not have erred in your Excellency's and his Excellency's judgment, all the more so since the aforementioned de Buck is always obligated to return here, and has had to leave his household here behind. The Reverend Cornelis Paijs had also previously endured various illnesses, but was at that time recovered to health, which gave us hope for his continuation; however, since then, to our sorrow, it has come to pass that there was great doubt about his recovery, and he now seems somewhat better, but nevertheless also runs the risk of lameness. The sick man and treasurer in the sick house, Jacob Seits, was buried the day before yesterday after a short burning fever. The affairs on Ceram, for the most part, proceed on the same footing as we have previously mentioned, except that between the Sultan Lissebatta and Raja Sahulau, regarding the conduct of their affairs, some difference and irregularity has arisen, which one will endeavor to settle as much as possible.

The affairs on Ceram, for the most part, proceed on the same footing as we have previously mentioned, except that between the Sultan Lissebatta and Raja Sahulau, regarding the conduct of their affairs, some difference and irregularity has arisen, which one will endeavor to settle as much as possible. Two Moorish priests from Hitoe have also conducted themselves too presumptuously, converting heathens near Hatuwe to their sect, which guests have been summoned by letter sent to the Orange Kaijen there; another one, now lying sick in Bonoa, shall also be dealt with regarding this matter. On the 10th and 21st of July, two fortified vessels appeared here from the eastern side with approximately 140 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 8,400 kg] of massoy, which he sold to the burghers at 10 to 11 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] per picol. With the White Lion, your Excellency is to be served: the requested masts and spars, as they lie loaded therein for ballast—56 pieces [modern equivalent: uncertain], which perhaps will prove to be of better quality than we had thought. Neither Meliskerken nor Hilversum could take any of them on account of lack of cargo space. With this, your Excellency, most esteemed, highly honorable, wise, provident, and most generous gentlemen, etc., your Excellency's faithful, obedient, and humble servants signed: Anthony Hurdt, Paulus Andriesz, Willem van Zeijl, absent Gerrit van Voorburgh. At that time in Amboina in the Castle Victoria on the 13th of August 1668.

text_translated_detailed: 25 May. Report of the true condition of the redoubts and outer guards on the coast of Hitoe, the islands Honimoa, Oma, Nusa, the land and Pass Bagnale, containing their locations, strength of the garrisons, war munitions, and furthermore everything that depends thereon, delivered in writing by Captain Paulus Andriesz, expressly commissioned for this inspection, to the Venerable Anthony Hurdt, Chief Merchant and provisional governor over the province of Amboina with its jurisdiction. It was on the 25th of the previous month of May that I took my leave of your Excellency, and with the Corcor Unremessing, which was anchored in front of the Castle, I departed in order to carry out your Excellency's order regarding the inspection of the redoubts on and along the coast of Hitoe, the islands Honimoa, Oma, Misselant, and Passo Baquele, concerning their locations, strengths of the garrisons, etc. When in the evening we came to anchor in the Portuguese bay, where we remained that night, the next morning we departed again toward the redoubt Rotterdam on Larique, which after inspection we found to be occupied, provisioned, and conditioned in line as follows. 26th, same date: strength of the garrison: 1 under Merchant Jacob van Nes, 1 Surgeon, 2 Corporals, 22 soldier-servants, 1 musketeer, 1 carpenter, 28 Coppens [uncertain: possibly a unit of measurement or type of soldier]. Artillery, war munitions, and military equipment: 8 pieces of cannon, namely 2 shooting 8 pounds, 3 [pieces] 6 pounds, 2 [pieces] 3 pounds, 1 [piece] 1 pound of metal. Among these are two pieces of 8 pounds and one of 6 pounds that are unfit, because the touch holes are too wide, so that the powder burns out the back through them to the powder magazine, for which reason three others must necessarily be sent in their place. 2 metal basins, 1500 pounds of powder, 2 powder horns, 5 powder chambers, 49 hand grenades, 2 drills, 4 pieces of hatchets, 556 pieces of round shot, 6 lathe priming tools, 16 muskets, 54 pieces of long shot, 8 slow match sticks, 8 wooden cartridge cases, 9 half [measures], 1700 musket balls.

The merchant Adriaen, having order from here to inform himself on various matters of the Ceramers on this side, has just sent us the report inserted in the incoming letter page 54, to which, to be brief, we have respectfully attended. Since for some time now the flight of slaves has been very much in vogue here, and we have found that there was great inducement to this, the general negligence and carelessness regarding the light vessels, we have, after prior careful deliberation, deemed it good to devise and publish such a placard on the proper securing and watching of the aforesaid vessels, as is inserted under the resolution dated July 10, hoping that your well-honored will confirm the same with your approbation. Those from the village of Laijn have only brought forth some old plates, rings and gongs. These items Kackialij had hidden in his mountains and accessible hideouts. When he began the great revolt in the year 1642, waging war against our state, in the village of Waccal four persons were also found, whom Pattingij declared to be slaves. These people, having now lived there as free inhabitants for so many years, planted nails, and performed all other services, say they are properly not slaves, but were bound to Kackialij on account of debt. They have, however, according to their ability, brought forth something, with express declaration, just as all others did, that they bring these things forth with great hardship, not for Pattingij's sake, whom they do not wish to know and whose father with his harmful proceedings has brought ruin upon them and the common good, but in order obediently to follow the order of the Honored Lord General. With further humble request that they might be freed once and for all from Pattingij and others of that ilk remaining and still dwelling in Batavia, the Ambonese, from their unfounded petitions. Since the things brought forth were partly rags and could not have been transported on the ships without damage, they have been converted to money,

text_translated_detailed: has brought ruin upon them and the common good, but in order obediently to follow the order of the Honored Lord General. With further humble request that they might be freed once and for all from Pattingij and others of that ilk remaining and still dwelling in Batavia, the Ambonese, from their unfounded petitions. Since the things brought forth were partly rags and could not have been transported on the ships without damage, they have been converted to money and have yielded 160½ rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] at 60 stuivers [modern equivalent: Dutch currency], among which are included 70 rixdollars which Entsje Taij paid for a certain slave woman named Manis with her son Adam, formerly belonging to the aforementioned Kackialij. The aforementioned 160½ rixdollars has then been counted by the aforementioned Entsje Taij as procurator of Pattingij here in the cash box, to be reimbursed to Pattingij in Batavia. Thereupon adding two red silk cloths with gold stripes bound in a bundle with a note thereon lying in the cash box, together with two open Moorish letters from Entsje Taij written in reply to the same Pattingij, wherein he declares that the inhabitants of the villages where Kackialij had hidden his furnishings will confirm with an oath that they know nothing more that came to Kackialij. A certain Hitoenese named Molodco has previously sold six persons for his own profit, which Pattingij claims as slaves, but Molodco says these belong to him, since he is as much of the captain of Hitoe's lineage as Pattingij is. He is therefore unwilling to pay them, nor to go to Batavia for their sake, and (speaking under correction) we also think that Pattingij scarcely merits that one should force these people against their will for his sake. This we have thus set forth at length at the request of the aforementioned people, your Honors please take this in good part.

text_translated_detailed: Order and Instruction for the under-merchant and fiscal Marten Roos going as Commander and chief with the sloop Loenen and the small boats Valing and Diamant toward Kisser and the Eastern Islands. Since it has been reported to us both through oral and accompanying written reports from Sergeant Johan Blinne and quartermaster Pieter Slaager, who arrived here on the 23rd of this month from the island of Kisser, coast of Relewaen Damme, that some Portuguese from Larentouca, Macassarese, and others have overpowered the island of Kisser, burned everything, destroyed it, and carried away what they could, and also did not spare, as one would expect from the Company's faithful allies, the orange-cay Backer, namely, and the orange-cay Menoutij, treating them very harshly and carrying away the Company's effects in a hostile manner, claiming that they had been here in Banda with us the previous year and had placed themselves under the banner of the Honorable Company. Therefore, we and our council, after careful deliberation, have deemed it good to dispatch the sloop Loenen and the small boats Valing and Diamant with all speed with 106 selected soldiers and sailors, in the hope and trust that we shall find these aggressors on one of the three Eastern islands, Letij, Moa, or Laccar. And since for the execution of this exploit there is need of a person of sufficient experience and capability, we have, with our council, chosen your Excellency for this purpose, not doubting that you will know how to pursue our good intention in conformity with this our instruction and with the advice of the council. text_translated_detailed: Having made an opening in it and seen the poor condition, we have deemed it good to break down all the bad interior work, widen the outer wall, and provide it with a sufficient guardhouse [fortified structure] of approximately 6 feet filled with earth, between a new road of the Corps de garde, and with which we are now occupied daily. Once this is done, the guardhouse on the N.W. side of the same fort must also be renewed like this one, and with this the fortress will be brought into proper and suitable condition. And once the housing above the warehouses has also been renewed, as soon as we shall have received the wood from Ceram, work will be begun, so that the island, namely Pulo Ay [Pulau Ai], will not need much more to be done for a considerable time, except that the inhabitants there lack fresh water, particularly during dry seasons. To remedy this lack, we have here already made trial twice by digging large wells, and although these have given us good hope, they have not succeeded well. Now we have encouraged the inhabitants (as mentioned before) during our last visit there to make a new attempt in the middle of the land under a height, with the promise of all assistance, and with this we are now occupied with new hope of good success, especially because in the digging we found a good quantity of fat clay in some places, like pottery clay, which we have ordered to be set aside separately, so that if the attempt fails, it can be used for dams to set up a stone well in the same dug well, in hopes of leading the rainwater flowing down from the mountain into it and preserving it. And if it should succeed, it would be no small benefit for that island.

And once the housing above the warehouses has also been renewed, as soon as we shall have received the wood from Ceram, work will be begun, so that the island, namely Pulo Ay Pulau Ai, will not need much more to be done for a considerable time, except that the inhabitants there lack fresh water, particularly during dry seasons. To remedy this lack, we have here already made trial twice by digging large wells, and although these have given us good hope, they have not succeeded well. Now we have encouraged the inhabitants (as mentioned before) during our last visit there to make a new attempt in the middle of the land under a height, with the promise of all assistance, and with this we are now occupied with new hope of good success, especially because in the digging we found a good quantity of fat clay in some places, like pottery clay, which we have ordered to be set aside separately, so that if the attempt fails, it can be used for dams to set up a stone well in the same dug well, in hopes of leading the rainwater flowing down from the mountain into it and preserving it. And if it should succeed, it would be no small benefit for that island.

text_translated_detailed: We intend in the coming days to visit the islands and trading posts round about once more, and to issue the necessary orders on everything. You have seen the report of the Honorable Cornelis Speelman, in his second written report to Your Excellencies regarding his visit made in this Banda province, in which he has seen fit to state that whenever the Governor makes visits to the remote trading posts, cannon shots are fired upon arrival and departure, and Your Excellencies further say that such is not so necessary in Banda for reasons of respect, et cetera. Had the said Honorable Speelman been pleased to speak with us or someone from our council in place of others about this matter, we would not have told him otherwise. The Governor has nowhere less pleasure than in unnecessary shooting, and he has expressed this to the heads of the trading posts several times and considers it one of his principal duties to ensure good care of the cannon and its equipment. He also says he knows of no other way than that Your Excellencies' general orders are that the cannon, having been loaded for six months, should be discharged for its preservation. It is true that from time to time some of the aforementioned heads and constables have been reminded that the cannon should be loaded and fired over, and should be discharged. And so when about two and a half years ago a piece burst, and thereby a gunner was wounded, who also died ten days later from the Courtse and spasmus (an uncommon sickness in Banda), and not from the wound, the Governor does not consider this should have been imputed to him, for such inconveniences are quite common, as they were also in former times and still occur daily, especially because rust has infected many pieces to such a thickness of about an inch all around that they cannot be properly charged with powder. Also, the touch-holes of most of the pieces in Banda are so corroded that a thickness of about an inch can be inserted into them, and it would have been Your Excellencies' great consideration to have been informed of this, because upon his arrival the visit of the trading posts and the escort to Amboina, with the firing of the cannon, were meant to honor him, so we consider that the same should not have drawn any consequences.

text_translated_detailed: In the year 1656 or 1657, a piece burst at Pulo Ay, killed a gunner, and sent a piece of iron into the air, which fell through the roof of the house in the fort, down to the lowest chamber beside the Honorable Wijns' residence. In the year 1659, another piece burst there and struck a mardijker [free Black or mixed-race person] standing in the village, his arm was torn off. And in the past year two opourien [uncertain: possibly a rank or position] burst. We are also not negligent in properly provisioning the redoubts behind the highland with gunpowder and other war ammunition, according to their constitution, which is uncommonly meager. The old redoubt lies commonly with 6 men and a corporal, which serves more as a guardhouse than to be able to do any force from it. Its powder magazine is built in the north and foully warehouse. There lie together on 2 points 6 pieces shooting 4 and 6 pounds, and at his Excellency's presence there was not more than 600 pounds of gunpowder provisioned. And behind the mountain of Commer, where ordinarily about 3000 pounds of powder lie in the redoubt, and can be brought by slaves in 1½ hours from the redoubt Commer in bamboo containers as much as can be brought to Waijer, and Ourien lies but about 2 hours from Lonthoir, so that all these fortresses, as soon as we receive any rumors of trouble, must also be provided with sufficient garrison, and we remain properly recommended for care over this. Yet since Your Excellencies judge that these should generally be provisioned somewhat more liberally, we shall very gladly follow Your Excellencies' good opinion, as also over their necessary repairs.

text_translated_detailed: The replanting of linga trees [nutmeg trees] here is not impossible, but if this were to happen, better and more sheltered places would need to be chosen than was done before. During the presence of the Honorable Josap van Dam in Banda, the park owners were required, for the license to make gardens in their parks, which must often be changed due to the scarcity of the soil, to plant a quantity of young nutmeg trees in the same gardens. But when we saw that these grew sufficiently in the forests from the fall of nuts in the wilderness, we judged it not necessary to have this observed so strictly. Now the park owners and those making gardens could well place the planting of linga trees in place of this burden, but we do not know whether this would have effect in Banda, where so little is planted, and if so, they would undoubtedly be cut down before they reached their proper growth, and used for their own purposes, in place of titis and other wood that is found here and there in the forests, which they mostly use for their carpentry. Therefore the Company would have little benefit from it. And since on the coast of Ceram, Bouro, and other islands lying nearby, more wood can be obtained than we need here, we consider it unnecessary, under Your Excellencies' good judgment and better opinion, to expend much effort on this. Regarding the aforementioned instruction we have also given to our fiscal Marten Roos, we have said concerning the 14 Dammese astagers [uncertain: possibly a type of worker or soldier], 6 of them Christian.

text_translated_detailed: And through those of Mr. Roos, Your Excellency will be shown his arrival and accomplishment at the island Letij, and how there the Portuguese from Larantuka with 18 to 19 Correcorres and fast vessels, except some small ones, with more than 400 men on the west point in a sandy bay at the shore under the favor of a cliff and fortification have lain in wait, and from these in approaching they were greeted in such a manner that 3 soldiers and a sailor remained dead on the spot, and besides that 8 more were wounded, of which one has since died. And when the next day some orangcayas [uncertain: possibly a local title or rank], the Company's allies, had come to us, the Portuguese raised the white flag and sent their commissioners to us. When asked about the cause of their hostile aggression, they excused themselves, saying they did not know that those of Kisser and Letij were the Company's allies, that their captain was Moor Anthony Ornay, a knight of the Order of Christ, and that the knight Francisco Viero had succeeded him in the government at Larantuka, and had departed with 12 Correcorres to Kisser to avenge himself for some damage suffered from them some years before. They requested that our Commander come ashore, under the assurance that satisfaction would be given for whatever damage was claimed by ours on behalf of the Honorable Company and its allies. This request was refused, and in response it was answered that if their chief could bring forward anything to excuse these vile deeds and robberies, he should then come himself to our Commander's ship, and if not, we would attempt to carry out our commission with armed force. text_translated_detailed: We have been informed by the Orang Caij Backer that in the Negrij Adij there are thirty Portuguese, who with the previous Company intended to go on a raid, but remained stranded there due to the misfortune of their vessel, and perhaps are still there. If it were not that eleven of the escaped Correcorren [local leaders] had passed by and given them notice, we would have decided to set our course directly toward the same Negrij Adij and further to ascertain how we would find matters there. Having in the meantime sent four of the Orang Caij Backer's Company with the Chialoup [small boat] Walinge to dispatch word to those of the Negrijs Wateroe and Weijma of our intention, so that they might come with some people by land to that place to prevent the Portuguese, if found on Adij, from fleeing inland. At six o'clock in the afternoon watch, we saw a black flag waving on shore, whereupon we deemed it advisable to come to anchor near them and to ascertain where the escaped rovers were. We set anchor at sunset near the Negrij Wateroe in nine fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 16.5 meters] of water on sand and clay ground. The Orang Caij of the Negrij, called Lebosje, came aboard at once and reported that the Portuguese who had escaped from us on the tide were lying on the Negrij Adij and had thrown up a fort there, because their vessels had been shot at very severely by us, and they were seeking to repair them, and that most of the inhabitants were against the Portuguese. He also informed us that on this coast near the Negrij Mannetoute there still lay a Dutch ship, whereupon we at once resolved to depart for the said Negrij Adij to see whether we could still seize the enemy there, especially since the aforementioned Lebosje promised our Orang Caij Backer that he and those of Weijma would go by land toward Adij and would be able to help us. We weighed our anchor, but the whole night passed with calm and fair weather. Saturday the 19th nothing further occurred than that we drifted in calm. Sunday the 20th in the morning with daylight we were a mile away from Adij, about a mile from the shore. Then the Orang Caij Backer steered ashore with our provisions keeper in our boat to ascertain from the inhabitants there where the Portuguese were, as the Orang Caij trusted they were nearby. The Orang Caij having been ashore for an hour or two and having spoken with the people there, they said that the Portuguese had fetched water there and had already departed five days ago without having made a fort there. Two o'clock before midday we came to anchor before Adij. In the evening the Orang Caij Sille Sappa from the Negrij Weijmassingh came aboard with some company and said that the Portuguese had been there five days before, had repaired their vessels, and had provisioned themselves with everything, but they had not heard of Captain Moor, over which the Portuguese had been very grieved. The Orang Caij supposed that they had departed with their ten vessels, without doubt toward Larentouke. text_translated_detailed: Batavia. To the Esteemed Mister Joan Maatzuijker, Governor General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen of the Council, Esteemed, earnest, highly honorable, courageous, well-informed, wise, prudent, and generous gentlemen of India. With the great ship the Hoff van Zeeland [Court of Zeeland], we have, as per the accompanying copy sent to you on the 29th of June, our last letter, which ship in the Lonthoirse Gat [strait], after its rudder (which had been damaged above when cast overboard) was repaired and righted again—from the other side not coming to listen due to the strong currents—was set against the Gounong Apij [mountain], so that we had enough to do to help it (with as many orangbaijs [local workers] as we could get ready) away from there again—which was no small matter of foresight on the part of the ship's officers, that they had not done this earlier, and with great luck besides. Before it went to sea, we had it sufficiently provisioned, and on the 6th of July it went to sea. text_translated_detailed: In the Negerij [settlement] Manatoute, a Moorish vessel from Makassar was found with a pass from His Excellency Admiral Cornelis Speelman. Initially, the machoda [captain] was left unmolested on account of this pass, but when the — houcker [small vessel] the Quicksteert passed by there, the Makassarese brought news of their breach of contract and new war. According to the enclosed resolution, we deemed it good to seize the same vessel at a fair price, and from its goods brought here: 3,520 pounds of wax, 15 elephant tusks, 4 hooves, 1 metal basin and a barrel of gunpowder, 14 muskets and two lontroers [slow matches], 10 slaves and slave women, 30 gongs, 70 Makassarese cloths, 20 red caricains [a type of cloth], 2 cases and one silk petticoat, 17 sticks of black amber, grey amber and amber noir, and some other clothing items. That Your Excellencies with the fluyt [ship] Pegu or Loene in the coming month, with spices from here, will depart to proceed to Makassar — the vessel being judged unfit to be brought to Banda — we have burned. We also found at the same settlement 2 Solorese vessels without passes, of which one had a prince's flag, both of which we allowed to sail away unmolested. It appears that the Massoij [nutmeg] trade with the East Cherommers [eastern traders] over two years has pleased them so well that this year there have been 14 vessels there, and although we are displeased that without our passes some vessels have gone with Massoij to Makassar, Bali, Java, and other places, we have nevertheless not failed to send back this month a large vessel with 8 pieces of cannon and 70 men mounted full of Massoij, and another one also loaded with Massoij to Lambock with the intention, as we were informed, to bring back war ammunition from there. Here we have had 2 vessels full of Massoij and still 2 more.

text_translated_detailed: To the Esteemed Lord Governor-General and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of India. Esteemed, earnest, most high-honored, wise, provident, and most generous lords. On the 8th of August, we have informed Your great honor with the Yacht of the Neiras, freedman Gabriel Nacke, recently sent, as may be seen by the copy attached hereto, and since no word from Your Excellencies has come to us since then, we shall conduct ourselves in all service to you. With said Gabriel, without our license, departed from here the Bandasen freedman Steven, a Spaniard, and after our fiscal had conducted the inspection of the said Yacht and had guided the same outside the Gunung Apij [Mount Apij] in lee, having separated from there, said Gabriel set it to the wind, and the same Spaniard in watch, who with a vessel that was manned by slaves, from the other side of the Gunung Apij, came out of the lonthoirle gate, on board, and so departed with him. Whether, as some think, they carried some spices with them, we cannot say, but if it were permitted to the Bandasen burgher to sail without strict inspection from here, there would be found enough who would not find themselves burdened in this. What was accomplished by our fiscal, Sir Marten Roos, on his conducted Z.O. [Zuid-Oost/Southeast] journey with the fluyt Loene and 2 chaloupes [small boats], shall Your Excellencies, with our previous report mostly already made clear, have received delivered to us. Your Excellencies now also receive here alongside, and the 2 Portuguese hostages go with this fluyt Loene to Makassar, and as we sent Your Excellencies in our last, the question points to them in the form of an interrogatory, so a copy of that is also attached hereto. We have provided said hostages with their necessities through a freedman, and being deprived of clothing.

text_translated_detailed: our previous report mostly already made clear, have received delivered to us. Your Excellencies now also receive here alongside, and the 2 Portuguese hostages go with this fluyt Loene to Makassar, and as we sent Your Excellencies in our last, the question points to them in the form of an interrogatory, so a copy of that is also attached hereto. We have provided said hostages with their necessities through a freedman, and being deprived of clothing, we have caused some to be procured, the one and the other amounts according to the account attached hereto: ƒ 162:-:- where the General Comptoir will be debited, we consider that His Excellency Admiral Cornelis Speelman will find occasion to be able to discharge him with restitution of them, in which case said item may well perhaps be settled again at His Excellency's General Comptoir. Now we intend to send our sloop Banda made here soon to the coast of Relewaen for the wax trade, and whatever else falls to be exported there, and to provide our garrison holders on Kisser with what is needed. What we shall be able to accomplish there will be advised to Your Excellencies with our next. The Yacht Jacatra will be entirely unserviceable to us in this province on account of its unfitness. It is undoubtedly too short in the stern. We intend to send it also against the going out of the Moullou to Damme and Nle to fetch sulfur, and to return here with the beginning of the west monsoon. If it could be lengthened 15 to 20 feet, it would undoubtedly be more suitable for the Company's service. A small belayed houcker of the smallest type would be of good service here for the navigation of the Z.O. [Southeast] islands, more than our chaloupes Walinge and Tijgers Eylanden [Tiger Islands]. They are worn out and unfit to sail further, and the diamantie is so small that it scarcely carries more than its water ballast.

text_translated_detailed: Order for the Venerable Maximiliaen de Jong, President over the Esteemed Company's affairs in the Moluccas, to direct himself according to further orders. Two memorials, one from the year 1656 by the Esteemed Jacob Hultoert, Governor, handed to the Esteemed President Simeon Cos, and the other by His Excellency in the year 1662, when he was Extraordinary Councillor of India and Governor with the Moluccan Command, placed in the hands of the aforesaid Commander Anthonij van Voorst, contain such a comprehensive account of the situation, lands, peoples, the nature of the Kings, and their officials, of the Esteemed Company's and the Castilian forts, of the trade, and furthermore everything else here in the Moluccas, that nothing more need be added, although various changes have indeed occurred between that time here, because the Spanish have abandoned all their forts and shipped them to Manila — for besides that you have been employed here in the Moluccas since the beginning of the year 1657 in various respectable positions, up to second person inclusive until 1662, so since then you have been in the neighboring province of Amboina as second in your office, so that you cannot be ignorant of any matters concerning this place, which having been observed by Their Excellencies the High Government of India, I have deemed it sufficient in my instruction — that you alone be furnished by the aforesaid Commander under my authority, with a memorial of those things which first and most necessarily should be provided for the service of the Company, and upon which His Excellency has meant to note that not everything that occurred and was decided in the resolution while my presence stood has been — and understood, which you have therefore been given in authentic copy, and moreover you will be able to remind yourself with the general letters that have come and gone, carefully reading through them,

text_translated_detailed: The practiced Spanish law, entirely removed in its entirety, and by these people according to their desire, has been subjected to the Company and placed under its protection. The greatest difficulty lies with Chiauw [Tidore], concerning the residence of two priests, how His Excellency understands this matter there, appears from the aforementioned letter. I consider that if Your Excellency goes to Manado once, you will be able to direct it from there with foresight, under the hand, to which end you will be able to do so, especially now that the defeat of the Macassarese is fresh, and thereby the Company's fear is all the greater, which, with further good success against those enemies under the gracious help of God, still stands to grow. The known faction and division on that Chiauw will be able to facilitate the matter. At the same time, the area will also need to be thoroughly searched again in abundance, whether there might also remain some nutmeg trees, or whether new shoots might emerge. The previous great expectation from Mindanao has indeed been quite poorly fulfilled, yet it is not unnecessary to maintain good relations with those people, appearing to be still fairly good Spanish, just as the Spaniards in that land also still claim some free jurisdiction, which should also be removed in this time. The translation through a letter sent by the Corregidor of Mindanao with his envoy to the Corregidor of Tidore is attached hereto, and from it can be seen how he presents it, the Tidorese having been released from the Spaniards, making them out as their common enemy. The time comes when that envoy from Tidore must return home again, and that with Your Excellency's communication. The letter must be answered, at which time it will be appropriate to reproach the Corregidor regarding the courtesy shown to Spanish priests in the past year, with an admonition to refrain from such correspondence, and rather to follow the example of him.

From Ternate through the President Maximilian de Jongh and the aforementioned council to Your Excellencies on the last day of the month. The said priests have already sent various letters to the president, the contents of which remain principally unknown to us, because they are written in very small and crooked letters, and here we have no one who can read them or translate them properly. For this reason, they have not yet been answered. There remains now the island of Tagelande, about four miles from Ceauw, lying on the same line. text_translated_detailed: Moluccas, by the Admiral's arrival, authorized by the Esteemed President, Coll[ege] Batavia. To the Esteemed Lord Joan Maetsuyker, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords, Councilors of India. Well Esteemed, generous Lords, highly commanding, respected Sirs and Lords—. Through various letters and at diverse times your Esteemed Honors have been informed in broad detail of all that has occurred in the matters of war against Macassar. So it remains for me to report to your Esteemed Honors my actions as province superintendent and commissioner in the respective eastern quarters, wherein I shall be able to be brief, because your Esteemed Honors have already received through the Nuijsenburgh all the resolutions taken under my commission, as well as the memorandum left with President Maximiliaen de Jongh in Ternate for his provisional guidance. In which everything is written out in broad detail regarding what has been done and left undone, so I shall conduct myself in all humble respect thereto from the outset, once and for all, and proceed to make a beginning. Here your Esteemed Honors are already informed that I arrived on the 13th of March with the Yacht Tertholen, and the Lord de Jongh three days before me. Subsequently the entire fleet also arrived. I came ashore and was received in good order, and was courteously welcomed by the King of Ternate. Immediately on the square before the church I made my commission known to the people in public, and therewith entered the small fort New Orangien, where the commander van Voorst, having been previously informed by a letter from Voorbouten with the Crab dated the 10th of February of his dismissal, also declared your Esteemed Honors' intention again by word of mouth and showed it in writing by Instruction, to which he submitted himself obediently and contentedly. text_translated_detailed: According to my limited knowledge, a sufficiently strong fortification in the Moluccas is necessarily required, and having considered this matter from various angles, I have not been able to find anything better or more cost-effective than the preservation of the old castle, and to carry out the necessary and required repairs to it, all with properly closed bastions or bulwarks, the curtain walls properly elevated and fitted with a suitable wall-walk, in such a manner that one can move along the same from one bastion to another and come to each other's aid, and also be able to clear the same walk from the bastions. The dwellings below in the castle are of no importance, as is evident from the report of the appointed commissioners, and a dwelling would need to be made for the commander below, and furthermore new warehouses would need to be added there. However, I believe that if one begins work there, the entire work within the castle could also be arranged in such good order and divided into such blocks that one could sweep the entire castle from within, both from the bastions as well as the curtain walls, straight and crosswise. And it would then, in my opinion, be better that everything be made solid and properly at once, than that one merely throw it together hastily and be forced to constant new repairs. Otherwise, a house for the Commander and warehouses should be made of stone, and the Moluccas certainly merit 300 to 350 military personnel. Also, that Colucco [Kolaka] might be held in occupation. Regarding the fortification on Macjan by the sea, all other dwellings could well be constructed of wood and thatch, and a tile roof laid upon them, but that is always something new—no sooner is one thing done than the other falls into decay again. The bastions, being closed off with sufficient wall-walks, the entire castle can, if need be, be defended with 100 brave men, and in difficult times everything that one trusts can be brought inside. Besides, there must always be able to be a strong garrison

text_translated_detailed: under Your Excellencies' correction, I cannot consider it ill-advised to have the fortification there sufficiently strengthened. The great bulwark of Fort Mauritius, situated on top of the mountain, had for the most part been rebuilt and brought into defense. As the carpentry work continues, a little more can still be done, and one might not unreasonably consider, in troubled times, to station some Dutchmen there for the garrison, to reassure the people of Macjan. There is still much to be done, for the water tank is reasonably adequate for storing water, and I have recommended there that the overgrown brush and scrubland that has grown up all around it, and where access is thickly overgrown, be cleared a little, to improve the view somewhat. On Baetjan [Bacan], shortly before my arrival, there had been no small earthquake, from which great damage was suffered in the Moor and Mardijker quarter. The king's house and temple, the Mardijker school and church were thrown to the ground. However, no damage of importance was done to the fortlet, and there would not have been much to repair here, if Ensign Michiel van Hasenbeecq, instead of attending to his own affairs, had conducted himself in his office and duty as a pious officer. One can describe with truth how entirely shamefully filthy and dirty, everywhere neglected, that fortlet was found. And yet the garrison commanders were able to testify that it now looked quite respectable there, the king of Baetjan himself having repeatedly admonished him to take better care of one thing and another, with the offer of his assistance in whatever might be needed for it. The same ensign was summoned by the commander van Voorst on particular matters before my arrival, and arrived just before my departure to Malaya, so that there was no time for him to be addressed by my fiscal. Thus he was not present in my presence on Baetjan, and was replaced there by Sergeant Gabriel Thijsz, who is reliable and of good reputation. He was instructed in everything he had to improve and repair. The king was recommended to provide what was required for it, which His Highness willingly accepted, and also the president, to send what was needed from Malaya as soon as he came home, which was arranged with the sergeant who was subsequently deported to Malaya. Necessary carpenters and workers—His Excellency has advised me that everything has been done, and the most necessary things have already been repaired. I cannot refrain from, given such poor conduct, degrading the same ensign to sergeant at 20 guilders [modern equivalent: approximately €200-250 in current value] in fact, with the order to have him serve in that capacity in Castle Orangien, under the authority of the governor. When the Honorable van Voorst was heard speaking about this here, he seemed very to lament the procedures of the resident there, the same being Sergeant Joan Baptista. He writes that the King of Almoera [Ternate region], not most of his people having withdrawn to the mountains, because of the aversion they said to have, from there on their land for the Company a stone redoubt to make, but he thought that this was merely an invention of the King's wicked nature, and that the common people, at his instigation out of fear of displeasing him otherwise, had put forward such claims. He had therefore traveled to Almoera, and on the 11th of December had summoned the resident. He had been in mutual conversation with the King, in which the King endeavored to excuse himself, saying he had not advised this withdrawal of his people, and that he was forced to follow them, but he and they did not desire war against the Company. Whereupon the Sergeant admonished him to keep his subjects to their proper duty, and if they were disobedient, he would assist him in that. The King declined to take anything forceful against his people at hand; he preferred to try to dispose them to it with goodness. And about this the Sergeant, according to his own account, spoke very provoking words with great threats to soon teach him his ungrateful villainies and break his neck along with his traitors. With this, rising up, he refused the hand which the King presented to him, having 6 musketeers fire off, saying this is for now the last time; when we see each other again it will sound different. With this the chiefs of some nearby villages stepped in between the two, to come to a mediation of the differences. By which means the King had undertaken to make visits from village to village and to admonish them for the good, of which nothing came to pass. The arrival of the King of Tagulande. We have thought it good not to prejudice anyone, that one has granted to the King of Tidore the voyage to the Papuan lands, insofar as they fall under his jurisdiction, under stipulated restriction alone. Nevertheless, I have not failed to recommend this matter to the President with all its weight and to admonish him seriously, that he should also, at a good opportunity, have the Goram islands and other islands thoroughly searched once more in abundance. Regarding and in the matter of building, etc., having thus far discoursed, it comes to pass to answer to the 3rd point of Your Excellency's recommendation, being the inspection to be taken of the horse stable: we have found the same solid and strong, and such that it will not need to be remade or repaired for a long time, so that the governor's order regarding the sale of meat seemed to us to accord best with the Company's maxim, declaring that with the making of the same no more necessary work was neglected, nor was it undertaken without the mutual good will of Jan van Aelmonde himself. It is not to be denied that it lies quite close, having been set back by Captain Poolman at 50 paces, and the gentleman Copes himself understands well that it could have been placed somewhat further; however, it is not the stable alone that lies so close, the court is at the same distance, and if the enemy comes so close, they will also be able to find their convenience in various other stone buildings, lying one as well as the other against the good order of fortification. 5th, regarding the distribution of the cattle among the landholders of the great land, it appears from the session of the 13th what conference I have had with the common burghers concerning this, Messrs. van der Straten, Pooleman and Gabbema were throughout present, and we could well see that only few complained more about this than was necessary, and that there was more jealousy and envy than harm among them, those who complained most scarcely knew themselves how they would have it, yet they were unanimous in the opinion that the beasts should be increased rather than diminished, upon which it was decided that each landholder shall be free to keep cattle according to the extent of his property as much as he can conveniently manage; provided that the largest in the land shall not exceed the number of 30 to 35. Being hereby also settled the dispute over the cattle of Aert Anthonisz, whose children young and old were between 40 to 50 strong, this fellow does not have the gift of making himself agreeable to his fellow neighbors or others, and thereby it seems he has been given somewhat too broad a reputation, certainly the keeping of cattle in Banda is necessary, as one can draw good profit from keeping them, and especially in sickness as otherwise the burghers are very in need of some sweet or buttermilk. I think that for the great convenience of the Banda burghers, and without prejudice to anyone (having inquired about this, no reason to the contrary has been given to me), a good supply of cattle could be kept on Pulo Ai [Pulo Ai Island], and slaughtering could be done weekly from them, unless the Company itself did it, or if one kept the beasts in reserve

Canebij of the negerie Meloe, son of the orangcaij Lappaman. Thamlillij of the negerie Coba, son of orangcaij Pela. 14 individuals in total still living, for whom monthly payment is made from the Company's account to the governor for their maintenance of 4 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency], totaling 56 rixdollars. His Excellency had arranged this according to the custom there, for just as the lord of Dam had done the same for those who had been there in his time, they receive their sustenance from the governor's kitchen, consisting of rice and also fish, which they catch themselves, and otherwise they receive mackerel like others. They are clothed twice a year with a cotton breeches, which, as they themselves stated when appearing before us, has been noted down. So that (if one speaks the truth) the governor bears no burden for their maintenance. It may well be that the Dammanese are bound to their duty by the residence of these children at the castle Nussan, but I have a very small opinion of that, and the lord governor also believes with me that they will do or refrain from nothing on that account, except that it has occurred to me that in case they had evil intentions, it would be difficult to prevent most, if not all, of them from fleeing. His Excellency is of the opinion that the Dammanese, now that they are rewarded for what is imposed upon them to do, which they previously declared they had not enjoyed, although it has been provided, would not easily fall away again or play the beast; however, until now they have conducted themselves very well as servants and obedient. And from this one could think that the Company could save these 6 a

text_translated_detailed: he, through his own drive and sensuality, already had some guilt in this matter. Besides, that sort of people, in doing so, are brought into too high esteem, making the Ambonese find our rule somewhat palatable. Their assigned wages are enough. Which, according to the teaching of experience in those lands, is seldom of good effect, and I consider this gnatahoudij already to be brought into such high esteem that it is ample reason why I have left the council to recommend in this matter to moderate such a maxim somewhat. It is to be noted in the resolution fallen under the cession of 3 June that the raja of Titowaij and the pattij of abobboe absolutely accuse the same guatasoudij of having allowed himself to be corrupted by raja amet and the pattij of acone, when he was commissioned with the merchant from here and the pattij of alang, over a certain boundary dispute on Nussalut, between the parties in question, and over which I and the council have been forced to resolve anew, to have a commissioner sent there at the first opportunity, to remove the bitterness between these people, which was already growing high, through an impartial boundary demarcation. It is indeed good that one tries to make the Ambonese find our rule so palatable, so that they, upon the arrival of another nation, do not turn their heads toward change and toward another [power]; but that is not right, sir, to do with great leniency and even nearly as if relieving them of all servitude, or if they are used for work, to give them great wages. It is a people of such a nature that they think themselves most important when they are most honored. They necessarily require proper servitude and rightful subordination, for which the old experienced governors have laid down sufficiently good maxims, which no one need be ashamed to follow. And one will be able to assure oneself more of their loyalty in this manner than if one relieved them of all servitude. Therefore, the council together with me has thought that the wages, which Your Excellency has liberally seen fit to double for them, are abundantly enough, and that they need never be raised further. By me, with the advice of the council, as can be seen in the resolutions, only that change has been made, that the pangaijers [uncertain: possibly a local official or worker] instead of 2 pounds of rice, shall receive 1 pound of rice and 1 stuiver [small Dutch coin], otherwise they will still keep on begging for something for nothing as a side dish. But this is not further than upon Your Excellency's further approval, as Your Excellency has declined with very great foundation to the establishment of a weir [water barrier], which also is not very practicable. The moving of some villages on Hommoa [Homoea], from the Isamaauwers and other rebellious Ambonese under the Roodenbergh, Manipas, is therefore unnecessary and no less disadvantageous. The concept was to place each one's gardens in perfect separation, which has caused endless disputes, besides that it was not well feasible through those wild forests, and therefore one need not think of such novelties hereafter.

Now you will be further advised under 20 September from Amboina how the Rajah of the islands Mexicol, subject to Tidore, by custom makes yearly in the bay of Hatuwe his contribution to be demanded, without further offending anyone, thinking that without this he would also again be unable to be able to bring his tax to the Tidorese. I consider that it will be most fitting that one, through the Honorable President de Jongh, make this known to His Majesty, to the end that he may instruct the king of Mexicol to cease imposing such burdens on the company's subject peoples, believing that if it is presented to him with discretion.

That he shall never fail to regulate himself according to the known orders of the Company, one of which is signed by him, especially that he shall not transgress against the 16th point thereof, and should anyone think that he had overstepped in this with any overly sharp applications, that he nonetheless has never intended, or thought to pique anyone in the world, especially not the Lord Governor, with regret that his Lordship has understood his good intentions so contrary to his wishes, which he will and shall bear according to duty and oath with all particular love, honor, respect, reverence, and submission. Also that he shall well avoid, according to the content of the 4th point, involving himself in civil disputes, just as he has never done until now, and should anyone think that it happened thus or was reported, he says in good conscience and faith to be innocent thereof, which he shall henceforth demonstrate with Christian admonition

The aforementioned Captain, then, returning in the afternoon around 4 o'clock, reported that when he came near the said vessel, and they also saw the shallops coming, they had lifted their anchor or drag, and tried to escape and flee with paddles and oars, as much as was possible, hoisting a white piece of cloth that they let wave. Our men, having overtaken them at the nearest point, had gestured and called to them that they should wait for the shallops, so that they could speak with them, and that no harm or injury would be done to them. They said they had something to say to the Lord Admiral, who was now sailing about here and visiting the islands, but they would not listen to that, but rowed all the more eagerly to get away. They would not allow anyone from our men to come to them with their small prau [boat] that they were towing with them, nor would they permit any of our men to come to their vessel, but called out that they were Ceramers [people from Ceram], and that they came from Goram, going thus without looking back or heeding anything, which our men, seeing that they would not speak with them, and that they themselves, although both shallops had not lain before his bow, could not prevent, resolved to fire a musket shot over the vessel, which was no sooner done than those from the Correcorre [vessel name] fired at our men from two cannons, or stone pieces.

text_original: Battavia Aan D' Ed:le Heer Joan maatsuijker Vn Gouverneur generael, en D' E. E: H. r Raaden van India Wel Ed.le achtbare genereuse Heer Den Heeren. Hoog achtbare Ed le Heeren. Onsen laasten van u Ed. e h: achtb. is gedateert den 12. october, ende den 13. en per 't hof van Zeelandt afgegaan, de copia is hier nevens gevoucht. zedert is radja palacca geadsisteert met de oppassers, ende comp. e van Iancker, terwijle noch 2 nederlantse Comp. e tot een reserve bijden hand waarn gerukt des anderen daags smergens bezuijden 't bos van batta batta, dicht onder de 1. pagger, in scherpe actie geweest, daar in de vijand in persoon door de Coninck ende alde groote aangemoedicht en wierdecontinueel met troupen ververcht„ zoo dat het gevecht hevich en inhand-gemeenschap geraakt was, daar goet danck d'onse het voordeel van weg droegen, hebbende over de 100. koppen bekomen, ende sijnder volgens de na verkrege rapporten, noch wel ruijm 100. wech gedragen, de gequeste ongereeckent, ons quam het 15. ende onder die 4 wackere kerels te kosten behalven 33. gequetsten, en een van de oppassers door de arm geschooten, wij hebben 't zedert verstaan dat soo wij vorder waaren ingedrongen, de vijant in't geheel soude zijn verjaecht ende wel licht de nieuwe pagger verlaten, dan 't was hoogmiddach, zeer heet 'tvolck vermoeijt en scheenen oock met dit verkregen voordeel wel vergenoeckht, ons gebleecken wesende dat het hun voor 't merendeel, al weder 't hart vrij wat onder de riem had gesteecken, 'smergens hier naar verthoonde sich de vijand onder verscheijde vendelen weder ter selven plaatse, dan wij en lieten niet toe dat men daar op uijtginge, om ander werck (voor die tijt nootsaakelijcker) te vervorderen, dus gingense met de hitte van de middach-son weder heen leuren. den 17en 17. en snachts. waaren

To the Honorable Lord Joan Maatsuiker, Governor General, and the Esteemed Honorable Lords, Council of India, Most Esteemed and Respectable Gentlemen. Most Esteemed Honorable Lords. Your last letter to us, dated the 12th of October, departed on the 13th via the court of Zeeland [Zeeland], and a copy is enclosed herewith. Since then, Raja Palacca has been assisted with the native soldiers and the company of Jancker, while two other Dutch companies were held in reserve. On the following morning, south of the forest of Batta Batta, near the first palisade, there was sharp combat, in which the enemy, encouraged in person by the King and all the great leaders, was continuously reinforced with troops, so that the fighting became fierce and came to close quarters. By God's grace, our men carried off the advantage, having obtained over 100 heads, and according to the reports subsequently received, they also carried away well over 100 more, not counting the wounded. We lost 15 men on the 15th, and among them 4 brave fellows, besides 33 wounded, and one of the native soldiers was shot in the arm. We have since understood that if we had pressed further forward, the enemy would have been completely routed and would likely have abandoned the new palisade entirely. However, it was high noon, very hot, the troops were weary, and they also seemed satisfied with the advantage gained. It became clear to us that for the most part their courage had already sunk considerably beneath their belts. The following morning, the enemy appeared again under various banners at the same place, but we did not allow anyone to go out against them, in order to pursue other work (which was more necessary at that time), so they went away again in the heat of the midday sun. We have since understood that if we had pressed further forward, the enemy would have been completely routed and would likely have abandoned the new palisade entirely. However, it was high noon, very hot, the troops were weary, and they also seemed satisfied with the advantage gained. It became clear to us that for the most part their courage had already sunk considerably beneath their belts. The following morning, the enemy appeared again under various banners at the same place, but we did not allow anyone to go out against them, in order to pursue other work (which was more necessary at that time), so they went away again in the heat of the midday sun. text_translated_detailed: again out on a raiding expedition, but they were discovered far too early. Having made the last plunder on the 10th, the enemy had posted sharp and strong guards everywhere, so that now, having accomplished nothing, with some houses burned to coals, they returned. In view of the fact that all the women and children from hereabouts had been brought to other villages for better security, and since now for the first time with this plundering there was no more to be gained, by day some small parties went out against each other, in which now from one side and then from the other, a head or two or three was won and lost. So the thoughts turned again to the lower palisade, near Raja Palacca, which from the outside seemed somewhat damaged by the shooting of two or three coconut trees, so that another 8-pound cannon was dragged there. Between the 22nd and 23rd of October, at night, they went at it for the third time, meeting with reasonable resistance, but with the throwing of that fire weapon it was soon overcome. From the spilled blood, one could discern that damage must have been inflicted on the enemy, which was subsequently estimated by us at 30 dead. The garrison was between 300 and 400 men strong and had been commanded by Galeran Manassa, a Makassar man, in great trust by his king. A woman and a boy were found there. Furthermore: 1 standard, 2 flags, 1 fine metal cannon, 2 small metal swivel guns, 10 pounds of gunpowder, 20 muskets and musket pouches, and 20 cannon balls, besides some sharp weapons that they had gathered here and there from our cannon fire. text_translated_detailed: with a retinue of 50 men armed only with krises, toward the King, and they were received in every respect respectfully and with propriety, also by the King himself on an open balcony in the presence of most of the great ones except Crani Tello, who was on the Soupadon, heard, and there the letter was read, which according to the observation of our commissioners, caused deep consideration, being read by Calamatta, Finally the King answered; that according to the custom of the land on Makassar requested 3 days of deliberation, and between that time a cessation of arms from both sides, so that from the same he would send his answer, our Butonese allies sustained that one could not object to that and we made no difficulty in it either, so to that end the order was first established and we strengthened ourselves as well as the enemy meanwhile as much as time and opportunity could allow, it was a wonder to see how ours and the Makassarese continually ran to speak with each other, one had his father, another again his brother, uncle nephew and such like blood relations, it being not the intention of Your Excellency in this to weary you with an ample narrative of all reports that were brought to us between that time, this seemed most to agree that the Makassarese council, forced by the 3 known captains Tello, Poppoe, and Lincques, would not hear any request for peace, however much the entire community, the King himself, and various other great ones inclined to it, but of their vigorous intention to attack us from all sides with a general force, so little came to pass as we had little believed of it. Finally on the first of November around 11 o'clock in the morning came the Makassarese envoys followed by well 200 men, they were received in the field at the height in a pitched tent, and Messrs. van der Straate with Captain du Pon accompanied by Raja Soping with a retinue of 25 soldiers were sent there, to ascertain whether they besides the letter had anything to say orally, and whether they had orders to deliver the letter only into the Admiral's own hands, they said they had no other task than to deliver the letter, and showed themselves ready to do so, thus the same was accepted, and brought by the Captain du Pon to the Palisade, where one found it without the least courtesy, saying they did not know what satisfaction the Company desired, that the guilty Negroes for the murder committed against the Dutch be punished, and the yellow breach be paid and also restituted, which was in the wrecked Leeuwin found without more, which shall become clearer to Your Excellency by the translation itself, copied after the letter of our side sent to Makassar, receipted No. 3. text_translated_detailed: and Ian Jappan came out, reporting that his highness, upon receiving the message, had risen early and was already on his way to come out, when two Macassarese came to summon him to the court at the king's residence. When our people had taken their leave of him, he declared himself grieved that the ceasefire would not last another two or three days, but nevertheless that it would not hinder him from answering the letter and managing affairs further. We shall not involve ourselves in a recounting of all the back-and-forth conversations that occurred. This was solely the crux of the matter, sworn with solemn oaths and deep weeping, that he, now being assured of mercy and a general forgetting, would not remain longer with the Macassarese, unless he should come to flee in some vessel with all his people, or unless he should place himself under the protection of the king alongside the Malays in one of the forts, so as not to act there according to the Company's pleasure. And since he is in trust and seen favorably by the greater part of that nation, as having been faithful, except for the sister of Crani Tello, a Malay woman, with whom he has a daughter, under assured promises, that if not that very night, then at the latest the following one, he would send word and notification, whether by land or water—one need only arrange orders for the ships, that if a small prau came into the fleet at night, it should not be molested. Among the natives here there are various opinions—one takes it thus, another so—we keep our judgment still in suspense, and we are most astonished, since he certainly lacks no opportunity that, if he means well, he would not send someone with some message. text_translated_detailed: When he was captured and brought bound before the king (after he had slept off his intoxication), His Highness, hearing that he was an Englishman, sent him to the English, where he now is. He is an extremely drunk fellow, but nonetheless suspected of being as much of a scoundrel as he has shown himself to be in this matter, for from his reports made there, one can evidently conclude that he allowed himself to be found otherwise. For on the enemy's side in this war, no quarter is given to anyone who is found; he loses his head. And although our men have the duty to keep alive those they can capture alive, this does not happen because they do not ask for quarter, and then one also has no trouble keeping them. While writing this, yesterday morning, envoys from the king and great men of Makassar, who had been held back, came when the admiral, having arrived in the forest of Aijen, gave them a public audience. Their message was of the same tenor as the letter they brought with them, and along with the same they laid down money matters. Your Excellency will receive the translation and with it the answer, which was first given orally to these messengers, but afterward was put in writing so that it might be properly and well understood. However, before this was written and translated, when it was already copied out again, it was already around five o'clock in the afternoon, so our envoys first appeared in darkness at the king's encampment, where they were received with good decorum and brought to a suitable place. On behalf of the king, they were informed by Crani Ierenica, brother of Linques, that the King was inclined to receive the letter in person, but was now at his rest and could not come out. Also, contrary to their custom, he could not allow them to come inside. They wished therefore to interpret this in the best way and to excuse him to the admiral with heartfelt greetings. Coming tomorrow as early as it pleased them, thus the messengers returned with the letter. To the Makassarese delegation, it was said orally, as stands in the letter, that they should bring word before six o'clock in the evening what the king's resolution was on our answer. This did not follow, so we can well believe that they do not yet wish to resolve to send such commissioners as are required. Meanwhile, word came to us through a deserter that news had come from Couratta that the Cranis Laijo and Bancala were already on their feet, having placed the village palings under the king of Makassar in readiness, and furthermore had made their men ready toward Linques, where Crain Linques bears his name. Thus this force of 300 men had marched there in the afternoon, which is not a force to do any violence, but it is to be thought that the main intention will be, through his presence, to settle the people there and to deter them from defection. And although our raja here did not see much apparent danger in this and made the least difficulty of it, nevertheless the admiral found it necessary to send a well-experienced Buginese messenger by the small boat Dolphin there.
