text_translated_detailed: Which is not a force to do any violence, but it is to be thought that the main intention will be, through his presence, to settle the people there and to deter them from defection. And although our raja here did not see much apparent danger in this and made the least difficulty of it, nevertheless the admiral found it necessary to send a well-experienced Buginese messenger by the small boat Dolphin there to dispatch, in order to exhort them to courage with communication of the Makassarese letter and our answer given thereupon, along with assurance of the Company's good intentions and care for them. It is certain that the enemy, and the defection of these peoples, is apprehended according to its weight, for it is to be held as certain that if they come to us, our men do not doubt that concerning others it will be of bad consequence for the enemy, and therefore we believe almost that this aforementioned delegation to us has been made with an outward manner of satisfaction, without it having anything in fact, only to hold us off somewhat and to do their advantage under this, against which we keep a watchful eye. Being by the reckoning of the monies that the Makassarese messengers were supposed to take back, yet they were found to have laid down 3,394 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch silver coins] of the eighth inspection, good Moluccan. I think that each sack was sent for 500 Rixdollars and that the carriers had lightened it somewhat from their load. The finding by the appointed [official] is signed. It goes in certified copy here attached, and it will not trouble us to keep this fine money also for the Company, unless they should come back to fetch it. But then it will still be to be seen whether they will get it or not.

Two praus with Bugis have today in the forenoon from Maritson come fleeing hither, they report that there were no ten Macassarese in garrison, and that all Macassar was merely calling for peace. A good Malay scribe will be very necessary to us, the one we previously had was poorly worth his keep in that service, and he has also already departed to Batavia on account of illness, if he could also manage the Portuguese language, it would be all the better; this one will be brought to Your Excellency with the hooker the Quicastaart [ship name], which through the intervening conflicts with the enemy has been delayed some eight days in its departure, but we may not hold it up any longer now; whatever of importance occurs hereafter meriting an express report, we shall be able to make known to Your Excellency with one of our shallops [chialoupen]; meanwhile we request that Your Excellency have this serviceable little ship with its skipper, an untiring capable seaman, first cleaned up somewhat and then well supplied with anchor rope etcetera, be pleased to let it come back to us first via Japara [Japara], for one can do with it what one will, the accounts of the people are closed in order to be re-entered in Batavia, in view of the fact that no books are kept on the hooker, departing from Batavia the accounts of those whose accounts are closed there can be begun again in the books of Verthoolen, to the avoidance of confusion and much searching. text_translated_detailed: To the Honored Gentlemen, the Lord Joan Maatsuijker, Governor-General, and the Honored Lords, the Council of India. Your Honored Excellencies, Most Esteemed, Highly Respected, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Gentlemen and Lords, My Commanding Masters. Since Almighty God has been pleased to bless the Company's affairs under Your Excellencies' feared governance through the wise and prudent conduct of His Excellency the most generous and valiant Lord Admiral Cornelis Speelman, so graciously that this proud enemy of the Company's most precious possessions, the eastern provinces, has been so utterly humbled by God's grace that he has been forced to seek peace and, by the known contract between the parties and with Your Excellencies' approval, concluded here, has so far bowed himself that among other things one of his principal forts has had to be surrendered to the Company as its own possession. This conquest will undoubtedly be continuously garrisoned by Your Excellencies' garrisons, over which one of Your Excellencies' servants, as commander, shall govern under Your Excellencies' wise direction by Your Excellencies' favor. And since the aforementioned Admiral has been pleased to benefit me with the command provisionally and pending further consent from Your Well Honored Excellencies, Your Well Honored Excellencies' humble though faithful and obedient servant now presents himself to you hereby with the most dutiful request that Your Excellencies would graciously dispose matters to his advantage, assuring Your Excellencies that in duty and obligation I shall conduct myself according to my abilities such that Your Excellencies shall have no cause at any time to have had me serve through false and malicious service. Awaiting this from Your Excellencies henceforth, I shall meanwhile pray to God that He may be pleased to pour out His grace and blessing ever more abundantly upon Your Excellencies' wide and praiseworthy governance.

text_translated_detailed: Caijelij was shipped, and with it they were sent together to the roadstead before our fort, with Captain Duhon and Fiscal Gabbema being commissioned, along with the young Caijo, to say that they were going to the English lodge and to assure them, and if the Honorable [Governor] also wished to have someone sent on his behalf, then His Highness was in Goa, thus they addressed themselves to Stonto and Hinqus, where two of the King's interpreters were ordered to go as well, and also with the recommendation to be cautious along the way. On the way they encountered an Englishman sent by the resident with a letter to us, but the commissioners returned it unread. It was received outside the lodge by the second person, and the chief received it on the square where everyone was armed. They came by boat, and the Malays living round about likewise, but when they had understood the intention, they were willing to come as well, so the commissioners returned with the chief and the second person toward evening, having left under Corporal Backer six soldiers from the guards in the lodge, according to our order, for supervision, with the recommendation to them to avoid all insolence. These people, having come into our lodgement within the palisade, were still laden with great fear, but most of them were sent away with good treatment and a good drink, our address being that they should remain willing to submit themselves to the Company and Your Honors' authority, that they should honestly point out the Company's effects, and be prepared to be transported to Batavia [modern equivalent: Jakarta] as soon as possible, under the promise of all good treatment. They remained grateful, complaining about the Macassar rule, that they had been abandoned in such a manner, and moreover had been refused an audience. We gave them information that it could not have been otherwise, Your Honors,

text_translated_detailed: Caijo, at Stain Crenco, the evacuation of the Castle, the Admiral and Raja Pallacca having entrusted the care of the palisade to the head merchant of the streets and Captain Zuij steiger, having sailed with Feethoolen, Blauwe Visscher, and Goudeleuw toward here, with the Haeingh, Dolphijn, and Timos ordered to follow the next day. The next day they anchored the hooker before the English lodge, and His Excellency went there as well, setting in order everything for the goods to be recorded under a detailed accounting, to weigh, count, and ship, which proceeded in this manner until the 26th of this month, as appears from the attached findings, signed by the commissioners, in which everything is contained. And from there were shipped in the Heecker: three pieces of iron cannon of 6 and 4 pound caliber, two large and one small metal base with four chambers, 200 pieces of round shot sorted from our discarded cannonballs, one dumb tackle, one anchor dredge, 26,410 cattis [modern equivalent: approximately 35,200 pounds] of sapanwood, 14,880 cattis of very fine sandalwood in 446 pieces. In Nieuwendam, 31,735 cattis of sandalwood in 713 pieces, 582 cattis of elephant ivory in 34 pairs, 1,904 cattis of tortoiseshell horn, 17,556 cattis of cassia lingua, with which both small ships are crammed full. Six natural Englishmen are divided among them. On Nieuwendam, the chief with two boys, on the Prins Hendrik the second with two boys, Pr. Henry Pearle, Willem Stortingh from London, their master, and Jan Boon from Essex, trumpeter on the hooker, Patchevaal, stemming from London, assisted by two boys, Giou Kellij from Adselon, boatswain. Their private goods with Company books and papers had been sent with an express vessel on the 27th, 88 days after the enemy had been driven from the field by us, to Bantham, and it was also intended that they themselves go along. The rest we have allowed them to keep in their own possession, because it was of little importance, and yet a record was made of it nonetheless, as also of what had been left from their warehouses to various Malays, who under oath presented themselves to declare that it belonged to them, and that they had only had it for the accommodation of housing. We were more inclined to consent to this, and because it was also not of great importance, except that we would not be unwilling to obligate the Malays to us somewhat, by the declaration of the Commissioners, that we have attached to this, Your Honors would be able to perceive how gladly we would have taken a resumption of what had been found and noted in the lodge all since, in order thereafter to demand clarification whether also anything else for and on behalf of the English Company was resting somewhere. But they remained just as unwilling and stubbornly halting in the one as in the other, saying that because of the lack of books they now do not know, but that they would be able to make a correct accounting from the books to their superiors on Bantam, admitting nonetheless, as if according to their recollection, well 90 pieces of sandalwood more should be than our commissioners have found. Yet Your Honors will see how specious a declaration has been made by the same commissioners on the inventory, to verify that everything has been handled in good faith and carefully, regarding which we also have no reason to doubt them.

text_translated_detailed: Coromandel Coast, Superintendent and Commissioner over the eastern provinces, Admiral and Commander-in-Chief (and war power) over the ships. To all those who shall see or hear read our open letters, greetings. Know that the Prince Kalamata, moved with remorse over his committed disloyalty and misdeeds, both against his lawful Lord, the Earl of Ternate, his brother, as against the state of the general united Dutch chartered East India Company, since his flight in the year 1655 from the island of Buru to the Makassarese, until this present time, has shown himself willing on several occasions under this fluctuating war and particularly under the made cessation of arms, to be able to enjoy, for himself and all his people, so far as any still remained to him, an eternal forgetting, remission, and pardon. Being finally, on the 20th of this month, two days after the closing of the peace with Makassar, in person before His Highness the Earl, as before us, with a part of his people, entirely disarmed, come to humble himself. Furthermore, a continuation on the 24th, within these ships, to His Majesty and the general Company in our hands, with the nobles Panawa and Kalonga of Hualaba and Salo, the Qumeleka in the court of Thalatou, the Groffa Manieas, Malita, and Macacai of Siguo and Tabela, the Captain Poffigogo, the Lieutenant Moujaaure, the Ensign Godia, Saban, the Sergeants Toumat, Sousousou, and Cana Java, together with such soldiers as are hereby named, upon invocation of the Lord's name on the Quran, most solemnly and willingly and unforced, have made a special oath of all loyalty and obedience to their Lord and the Company. So it is that, by virtue of the power granted to us by the high government of India through open commission for the performance of all Company affairs here, with the advice of.

text_translated_detailed: name of His Excellency aforesaid, making known that whereas they at the time of the inventorying and taking up of their goods did not wish to be present, or had wished to involve themselves in any way with it, that they, as now from the authentic copy such as was found in the lodge, could obtain and resume, in order then further in good conscience to declare and affirm that in our hands no other goods have been shown and left, than those specified thereon, or that also no other further goods on account of their masters under this or that were here in the land resting, hidden or outstanding, which they had forgotten to give up, with the request that now likewise it would please them to do and also make known to us which persons were still indebted to their Company, with indication of where one would find those people, and how much they had to pay them, so that it would all come to light how justly His Excellency had dealt with and treated them, which would serve to the satisfaction and contentment of both parties and the settlement of the speech of His more esteemed Excellency, whereupon they answered that the copy of the taking up was not necessary, and therefore they did not wish to accept the same; as for the goods, they had given everything to ours, and held nothing back, but since they had sent all their books and papers by a vessel to Bantam, they could not give us notice whether our taking up had been done correctly, until they themselves had them in hand. However, they gave notice that on the Sandalwood about and near 12,000 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 5,400 kg] according to their account came short, their outstanding debts were of no importance. Two or three persons still stood somewhat in debt, but how much the same came to amount to, and where the aforementioned people were currently staying, was to them uncertain on account of having no books or papers in hand, consequently they could not declare the same with true conscience according to the truth, requesting that one would accept what was said as such, and cause them no further trouble on account of it. With this act they took their leave and the same having been reported to His Excellency, His Excellency ordered us again to go, together with the captains Pieter Coopman and Dirck van Rijn, as well as the bookkeeper Joseph Palacko, who had stood as expressly commissioned over the taking up of their goods, to come to them again to demand a clear declaration of everything which they, on behalf of the English Company at this place, had given over to them, possessed; at the same time pointing out to us and handing over again a certain Willem Willemse of Delft, Trumpeter, who during this war had gone over to them, and whom they, according to their admission, had housed for some days, or if he were too difficult, then they themselves with an oath would have to purge themselves that they were unaware of it; nor had it been done by their counsel. This being put before them again, they persisted in their first statement, without being able to add anything else to it. text_translated_detailed: Batavia: To the Honorable Mister Joan Maatzuijker, Governor General and the Honorable Gentlemen Councillors of India: Well-honored, highly esteemed, wise and valiant Makassar, generous lord and gentlemen, by the Honorable Mister Cornelis Speelman and the council there, addressed to your Honors on the 30th of April 1668: Honorable, high commanding gentlemen, under the 4th and 5th of December our latest dispatch per the yacht Nieuwendam and the hooker the crowned herring reached your Honors, and thereupon communicated what was then with the Chaloupe Timor and the yacht the Fortune toward Amboina and Ternate through us is mentioned: since then after long waiting, came first on the 30th of January here to the roadstead the fluyt High Caspel, with a good parcel of pork and cattle. Subsequently on the 8th of January the Cabellauw, the 18th and 20th of the same Claverskerke and Goerhee, and from the same the letters from the court of Zeeland and the fluyt Pegu, which was ordered to come to anchor in the bay of Furata at Toerata: further on the 5th of February the Chaloupe Tonijn, the 8th the Handelaer, the 11th Breuckelen, the 18th Hilversum and Leerdam, the 29th of the same the Quicksteert and White Lion, but the latter, unable to come in due to the stormy weather, was brought to anchor under the Herten Island, and from there the next day was again dispatched, but only on the 3rd of March could reach the Gong, finally on the 6th of March the yacht Meliskerke, the fluyt Loenen and the small boat the Caeuw, and now on the 27th and 28th of April the yachts Hogelonde and the Gelvisch, with all which ships we from your Honors have received your pleasant letters of the 30th of November, 23rd of December, 23rd of January, 19th of January, the 1st, 14th and 23rd of February and 23rd of March, likewise the copy of those of the 8th of January sent per the Pimpel

They have also given quite vigorous fire from the castle, though the ships but not the people were hit. text_translated_detailed: Batavia [modern: Jakarta]. text_translated_detailed: Batavia. To the Noble Lord Joan Maatzuijcker, Governor General, and the Noble Lords, the Gentlemen of the Council of India. Well-born, highly esteemed, wise gentlemen, very generous Lord and Lords, the highly commanding Lords. On the 21st of this month, with the burgher Andries Hartman, our last letter departed to your Excellency over the waters of Japara, of which we now send the copy herewith, to serve in place of the original in case it should be needed. Concerning the long-threatened attack of the enemy, of which we have been informed not only through some reports that have come over from various sources, but also through a Malay who dwells among the Malays, who was called to attention by night from meal to meal to the young nobleman, that it would go with great fury, has until now not fallen, and if one is to believe what has been heard for some days, it remains behind because of the little desire that the common man has in it. Meanwhile, both the outer works in that position have been brought along slowly, so that in case of courageous defense, for all their strength, there need not be feared. The Bugis have not yet completed theirs, but it seems now in some days to be done in their manner. If then the enemy is eager to take a prize again, they seem well able to endure it, and think that it would go very badly for them, their courage being somewhat improved through the arrival of about 500 men from the interior of the land, of which about 120 are old soldiers who have been present at the war on Ternate, having been under it, these having quite a bit of reputation above the common people. The Makassarese remain still quite quiet within their works, without one being able to perceive that anything is being worked on. Ours do also, each one does his best now and then.

text_translated_detailed: Meanwhile, with this gathering, daylight came upon them, whereby this good plan was abandoned. They are a wonderfully slow people and sluggish in their movements. Had Raja Palacca himself been there, or some few Dutchmen, it would likely have succeeded. However, to leave Raja out of his fort for a night would not be without peril, and as for sending Dutchmen along, it was not feasible since there was not enough people for the necessary garrison (as shall be reported further), from the Castle. Had the assault been well laid out and succeeded, it would have caused great disruption to the enemy at Marcus and around Tannete and perhaps a diversion, and would also have made the passage easy for our friends. On the same day when the Buginese were commanded to the aforementioned assault, in the sight of the enemies they departed with pack and baggage from the fort of Raja Palacca to the vessels. The Macassarese, as we presume, thought that the aforementioned fort of the Buginese was being abandoned, whereupon with a considerable force they came to investigate it, and were very bold in coming right up to the fort of Raja Palacca and that of Captain Joncker to show off their bravery, but were met in short order by the garrison with great courage, whereby certain great skirmishes, which lasted until evening, took place, and the enemy was attacked by our people in such a manner that they withdrew again with visible and certain damage. On our side, 5 men, both from Natanen and Amboinese, were wounded without peril and one Buginese remained dead. We have also had rumors here that Raja Pannawel with 3,000 strong was on his way from the south back here and had advanced to a certain village Lassij, but the Buginese place little faith in the great names of the few, and moreover nothing comes of it, such that it is to be reckoned merely as a rumor.

We shall therefore respond to the general with 60 guilders if we are not brought the cinnamon tree in reach. If Your Excellency with those ships, both from the fatherland and from the Cape, are richly provided with your seeds, please remember us: it will be charity and safe for the matter, for all that I sow here comes forth but we have nothing to sow. In the remaining goods of the surgeon Hans Voorregter, a silver shaving basin was found, which the ensign Berckman notified us belongs to the Company, being from the service that went with the lord of Hoorn to China. It weighs 20 rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 20 Dutch guilders]; for this the general has been credited to the amount of 60 guilders. Item, furthermore 86 rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 86 Dutch guilders] which were counted in cash by our fiscal, to be paid to Captain Poolma according to the bill of exchange. Against this we send with the Crabbe [ship name] according to the signed receipt 300 chickens, which have been brought to us from Ternate in reach, for 900 guilders, for which we have debited the general. The Ambonese who merely loaf about in Batavia, Joncker would gladly see them come here; if it is left to their choice, they will prefer to stay, but they must be absolutely commanded to do so. They come in very handy for bamboo and other work. Also, there are many stone workers in Batavia who have not much to do. Your Excellency, we are sending a party of them here and shall give them work. Ensign van Leenen, being very sick and imagining that he cannot settle well here, has not ceased to request permission to return to Batavia. text_translated_detailed: Colony Batavia. To the Esteemed and Honorable Lord Joan Maatsuijcker, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Honorable Lords, Councilors of India. Well-esteemed, most honorable, wise, valiant, most generous Lord and Lords, your most high commanding Majesties. In what capacity I have been sent on the voyage of the fluyt ships Goede Hoop and Hilversum, it has become clear to me that the Council, Your Excellency, with your double advices of the 27th of June with the same ships, has made known, as it seems to me, that you yourselves, to the Esteemed Honorable Lord General, through a small letter (whereby I may well say) my mission have notified. Thus, that I through weakness was not well able to perform my troubling function as required, nor could I well endure the continual address, much less serve in all things with adequate answer, was forced to convene the Council for my sleeping place and to show there how I was, as they knew, deprived of all strength and might, expecting: according to my feeling, on that very point rather an end of my life than an improvement of sickness, and therefore according to my small ability, having given them a sober address, I gave over the order sent to me by Your Excellency to be opened in case I came to die, with the order that the Council should not open it and direct themselves according to it, with which they departed well, but understood together that they could not do that as long as I lived, requesting that I would merely set the order, they would obey. Thus, knowing Your Excellency's intention, I have appointed the Esteemed van Diestraaten as chief overseer, to which he himself confirmed, and furthermore having left them the usual unity most heartily recommended. Thus, as during this expedition there has never been any misunderstanding between us, I went to the yacht Kogeland and therewith conducted a piece of the way from the roadstead.

text_translated_detailed: From His Excellency President Maximiliaan de Jong and the Chief Merchant Anthony Hurdt, provisionally acting as leader in Amboina, for the purpose that His Excellency would present them further to the vacant position, since they were aware that Your Excellency's intentions, with the turning of the monsoon, would dispose of it, His Excellency had already testified in private letters regarding their respective qualities, which we of the commission have attended to and have been present in all respects (as counselors), and we fully confirm that they, should Your Excellency and the Honorable Cops at Batavia come to appeal to the government, would be suitable governors for both governments, and likely no better will be found elsewhere, having already demonstrated in Ternate and the other in Amboina evident proof of how they, under their direction in all respects, have carefully attended to the service of the general company. Therefore His Excellency could not fail to serve you further in this regard with his testimony concerning Your Excellency, and to have them recommended to Your Excellency in the best form. Livinus Bor, where he came here with the militia, there was nothing lost, and he would have been able to proceed as a secretary, except for the lack of language skills, except that now again 2 or 3 lieutenants and quite a few ensigns are to be made, because the officers have also fallen away. His striving toward departure from Amboina is directed principally at this, because it has recently been spread about that he would be banished from Amboina for all his life, and that is however not appearing to be true, therefore such an unfavorable rumor cannot be tolerated. — For the horn work, our healthy Macassar stone was very useful but far too little, and similar ones came from Hommoa at 7 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] each, which is certainly too much there, but is good value elsewhere. With the restoration of peace, we will be able to send another ship's cargo of 2 or 3 of these without difficulty in commodity. The worst thing is that it is then just not the right season to fetch them from Pannakok and Barranbon, as it is in the northwest monsoon, what has been further communicated to us and written about from there is confirmed by the copies, to which we respectfully defer. — From Japara, along with the same cinnamon tree, 27 pillow [uncertain: original term] black sugar in 2 barrels has been brought to us, together with 100 pieces of rattan wood, totaling ƒ 132:—:— [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], which will also be properly credited to the general account. We bring against the general in return a charge to the burden of Japara of ƒ 4500:-:-: these are the 1500 reals or 3000 Macassar gold maesen [uncertain: original currency term], which Chiaeuco Gespans, captain of the Chinese at Macassar, has accepted from the company's resident at Japara, to be paid upon his appearance there, in fulfillment of 30 bahars [modern equivalent: a unit of weight, approximately 400 pounds] of sandalwood, at one hundred maesen per bahar, which the same had purchased just before the peace with the English resident. It was the Admiral who, in the time of peace, brought 40 bahars, but he always denied that, declaring 30 bahars and no more, but these had been paid by him, and he has persisted in this until now. However, he has finally condescended to pay the company, provided that he be given a receipt for the payment, so that, according to his claim, he might find a guarantee again with the English, which was readily granted to him, having then passed a debt acknowledgment before the chief merchant van der Strate and the fiscal Abraham Gabbema, a copy of which goes herewith, and of which an original is sent to Japara. We would have gladly had a surety or other security, but he could bring neither of the two, so we have held the junk of Annachoda Pitqus, with which it was shipped to Japara, here for so long, in order to go into the company of the waterhoen [uncertain: original term], of which the skipper has also been given his pass, to bind him all the more thereby to remain with him, somewhat as we believe from yes, it will still have been taken along with good. — Since our last, on the 5th of this month, the enemy first came according to most daily custom with some small troops from those who took their way toward Tello, but shortly thereafter with a burst showing themselves sufficiently the whole force in the field, holding us for some time in uncertainty as to where it would go, whether to Boutouale or to the whole, in both cases all necessary orders were first put in place and the watchers, 13 in number, with some boat commanders and Ternatan soldiers, were held ready to support where it might be necessary.

You, Your Excellency, can understand from the copy what was written there; furthermore, those people were well instructed in all matters and the letter was also translated very clearly into the Malay language. The day after, we first received news from a deserter that Chemmig had departed from here to Tello and was subsequently brought by Daijah Mangappa to Samboupo, where he was very welcome to the great one. He had reported that our works were already too strong to gain any advantage, but that the settlement of the Bugis lying at the Ternate quarter could easily be burned, swearing with drawn kris that he wanted to be the leader in that, and estimated that more damage would be done thereby than with the conquest of both Boulouwale and Talle. However, with the addition that both as well as our fort were completely stripped of people due to the sickness and death that prevailed among us. From Samboupo he was again escorted to Tello, but since then we have not been able to learn anything certain about him, it being believed that the Makassarese will try to guide him to Wadjo, so that from there he can travel safely to Luwu, where the same one could already cause some commotion.

He should only tell the king that they should hold themselves bravely and not hasten to make peace, for there had arrived a Chaloupe from Batavia which brought news of how the Mister General, being very disturbed with the Admiral over the breaking of the peace, sent another in his place to punish him, with whom they would then undoubtedly obtain better conditions in negotiation. Also noting that the people both in Tello and Samboupo were ready to attack Boulouwale that night or early in the morning. We had this Malay brought immediately and placed in custody, but he maintained his innocence. However, His Excellency heard him again a few days later, when he confessed that three days after the Englishman's arrival he had sent a letter to Tello to the aforementioned Daijah Anjo, but with not the slightest thought regarding such a matter. Nevertheless, this is the same time in which the Makassarese began to retreat in the pursuit of peace. If one may place any credence in the reports of this one and that one, the king and most all others incline toward it, but Crouron and the head of the Malay and Raja Lella, as most culpable in the breach, hold to it alone. But after the encounter of the 5th of this month, the great one began to murmur somewhat, but Crouron, causing it to be divulged, not only the arrival of Chemmig and that the same was evident proof that things were not going well with us, but that he had also obtained with the same assurance that most all the principal Bugis would follow in short order. With this they were again somewhat comforted. — We had sent a dispatch to Maros to inquire of some gallerans there, who were the true natives and land lords of that place, how they might now be inclined. Having previously, before we came to peace, shown the first good inclination to free themselves from the Makassarese and come over to us, our sent one from the garrison to confer with five of the most prominent, in which all consists. They made him a long recitation of complaints about all the bad treatment which they now more than ever before had to endure through this war of the Makassarese, and wished therefore that the war had been born, in which they might be freed from that slavery. This could not happen except with the help of our side. To this, if we might be inclined, they requested that one send some force to a certain place designated for that purpose, provided with a fine and open beach, and they would then as soon as they set foot on land join us with all their people, provided that one would free them and their property from the plundering and robbing of the Bugis. — Upon this, beyond all expectation, on the 6th of this month late in the evening, the young Soping of Zijan arrives with 5 small vessels but without a padijah [chief], having left the oversight of his people for so long under Arou Panna and Tobaecquij, reporting that after the last battle with Bone Songe, so that his people would not sit idle, he had sent a troop of roughly 500 men to the mountains twice, by which there so much commotion and burning of settlements had been caused. Coming with the same were the little kings of Sero, Malacca, Lipange, Todoncoere, and Pape, humbling themselves before him with a homage of 50 buffalo. He took from them the oath of loyalty to the Company and the Bugis subsequently provided them with safe conduct so that they would not be harmed by ours, who went out plundering here and there. And he had arranged for him and his people, by suitable routes over the mountains, behind the palisade of Bone Songe to be guided with one another, which would make up roughly 500 men to join with him, leaving as a pledge of their loyalty and good faith their women and children in such custody as he desired to place them there. With this he with the approval of the other chiefs was immediately dispatched to receive orders according to his oral report, what he was to do therein. They also said that by a troop of approximately 1000 men from Wodjant, sent by Daijah Macoule, the Makassarese envoy, to convoy Lamoera and from there to be safely sent to Makassar, the entire land of Sepingh had been burned without leaving a single house standing, being the

Batavia. To the Esteemed Lord Joan Maetsuijker, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords Council of India. Most Noble, highly esteemed, wise, valiant, and generous lord and lords.

Under date of the 19th of August last past, we sent you by the fluyt-ship the Waterhoen a small letter of considerable importance, and therein we discussed at length the state of the war situation here. It was also our intention at that time to have the yacht the Cinnamon Tree follow shortly thereafter to Batavia, so that Your Esteemed Lordship would long since have seen this without doubt. However, since circumstances have arisen in the service of the Company that prevented this resolution from taking effect, no further expedition to Batavia has followed since then, to which the indisposition of the Admiral has contributed considerably. He was struck down again at the beginning of September with extraordinary gravel and stomach pains, which have continued to the present day with little intermission and relief. Nevertheless, His Esteemed Lordship has remained in the field with the army since the 10th of September, without having returned to the Castle up to now, which we also considered very necessary in order to better keep the Bugis, who are entirely unwilling, in devotion and to maintain the work in this region, as on several occasions not only the common soldiers but also the very qualified Raja Pallacca had been left almost entirely alone, as he has made his complaints to His Esteemed Lordship on diverse occasions with tears in his eyes. text_translated_detailed: so otherwise it shall be done with reputation, that which necessarily must be done, for the firm establishment of the Company's state on this Island. And since Your Excellency is now given a complete opening in this matter, of the present military forces we shall henceforth defer the matter to Your Excellency, serving the Macassar, formerly so feared, now also not to be regarded as too insignificant, not so much for themselves as well for the rabble of Malays and their followers of all sorts, who with time have settled and taken root here, of which necessarily the most principal ones must be removed with the sword, then there will come a good peace, and it cannot happen without might and force, which being entrusted to us, the way being taken, Macassar we ourselves believe will rest well, for through the Malays and their firearms they have kept this entire people mostly in subjection and devotion. Here moreover we are also compelled to remind Your Excellency that extraordinary sailors must be sent, so that we can use the ships, which we so greatly need, in the service of the Company. Here besides go the Inventories of both the Vliekent Domburch as well as the Seahorse, from which can be seen what they have been provided with upon their departure from here. Your Excellency please regard this with eyes of discretion, being written in haste and with difficulty, with which then for the present breaking off, we commend Your Excellencies to God's protection and remain according to our respectful duty. Signed below. Most High and Commanding Excellencies. Your Excellencies' faithful servants, was signed Cornel: Speelman H:d: Bitter, Abraham Gabbema, Leendert Haringman, Poopman. at the side stood. In Maripou in the field the 14th October 1668. at the bottom stood. the remaining council persons in the Castle.

text_translated_detailed: it appeared to us that the poor administration there, and particularly of Crain Bancala, was the principal cause, and that the enemy had gained the best access to the minds of that people — and it now also becomes clear that the solicitations that came from that land to the aforementioned gentlemen should not be considered very reliable, since up to now, as far as we know, despite having taken up posts at the designated places and made them secure, only about one hundred men have come over at Crain Laaijo, and scarcely ten men at Crain Bancal, which is very much to be wondered at. The deep fear that the Macassarese have among those people is remarkable, being able to hold nearly the entire land in terror through the sending of one long, respectable person and a small retinue, under which burden they now still remain, notwithstanding that they have never been treated so badly before with the abduction of women and children along with other oppression as they have been during this war, yet they could now free themselves from it so easily. We have heard no further news since the last communication from those people, which we nevertheless still expect daily. The enemy accuses us in their letters, in which they speak somewhat boldly, that we have broken the peace, because on the 17th of April we first attacked them with weapons. Also, that we completely broke off the peace negotiations there. We can believe that Crouron would not have begun first on Macalse itself, being content in a state of strong defense, and under that favor being able to complete his underhand war, which was hindered for a while by our sharp vigilance that we maintained, so that then, as it pleased him, and we were least suspecting it, he would break out.

text_translated_detailed: During the peace, daily matters concerning this have been managed, and therefore we would prefer to dismiss all of them upon the restoration of peace and send them home. If it becomes timely with peace, the intention is to steer the old grain to Amboina and Banda, where it will bring a good price there. text_translated_detailed:
The chief officers of the ships recently arrived here from Batavia have undertaken to prepare the muster rolls of seafaring personnel who came with them back here, and with the first opportunity, both are to be sent to be brought ashore at Batavia by order of the fiscal [financial officer], the same being delivered here as Annex with their declaration regarding the allowance for the lightest of the suitable wages by the administrators at Batavia, as on each separate roll is specified and shown. The mustering has meanwhile been done by the fiscal and the military bookkeeper on all the ships that lie about here, correctly according to their ship's books and as is proper, finding on some of them already quite a poor state of affairs, because the personnel without their accounts [being] closed from one ship to another is, and has been ordered over, such that the same, also because the bookkeepers or the skippers and the clerks have been mostly sick for some time and some have already died from it, no correct records have been kept of whatever might be lost and missing. However, now after some days here, with the resumption of the aforesaid muster, comparing against one another and their books, much has been found and remedied, but there still remains nevertheless hidden, concerning people whose accounts still stand open in the books and in the fleet are not yet to be found, there is further search made, and that shall then also be corrected, being the same and those who here run on account [are] named and in the books of the following ships known, as

On Vertholen: Gerrit Hendrickse from Bremen, sailor for the Chamber of Zealand with N: [ship name] Middelburg, in the year 1665 came to India, is absent
Elias Adams from Stockholm, with Marseveen 6, for Amsterdam and boatswain, not to be found
Jacob

text_translated_detailed: To the Honored Sir Joan Maetsuycker, Governor-General, over all the Netherlands, and to the Honored Gentlemen, Councilors of India, Most Earnest, High and Esteemed, Wise, Prudent, Generous, and Strict Gentlemen. The Gentlemen's Yacht Muijden departed on the 13th of December in the year past with 294,000 cattis [unit of weight] of pepper amounting to ƒ 46,666/10 [guilders], we hope that it will arrive there speedily, and that our letters accompanying this and other papers will have been well delivered to you, Honored Sir. By which you, Honored Sir, will shortly have been pleased to see the condition and what pepper still remained in the warehouses. After which time, little of note or worthy of advice has occurred here, therefore this principally serves as an accompaniment to the notice of the departed vessels, both to Coromandel as to Malacca, since the 16th of May of the year before last, by which it can be seen whether those same have also arrived there well (as we have received word from Malacca), it will without all doubt not agree with our notation of their cargo, inasmuch as not everything the Company will declare at the closing of the toll, but necessarily more quantity has been brought there than is noted here. If they otherwise, as we hope, take the right course. Through the reasonable reduction in the Company's cloths which we had in the year before last and which seemed to follow in the coming year as well, we made a good request for the said cloths (because at that time we already had various sorts of cloth, which fell short for the trade), with which we remain to our great sorrow and amazement at present nearly stuck, being indeed the principal reason that several thousand men have been sent to the upper quarters against various rebellious villages that oppose the King in the river Commereijn, lying close to the Lamponder, or Toulongh Banwanger, as well as to make war against the same.

text_translated_detailed: To the Honorable Mister Joan Maetsuycker, Governor-General over all the Dutch in the Orient, and the Honorable Gentlemen Councilors of India. Most earnest, most honorable, most wise, most provident, generous, and strict gentlemen, your Honors. Our letter of the 5th past, sent by the King's envoy, we hope will have reached your Honors well upon receipt of this, but for greater certainty we send the copy herewith. Since then his Highness has also resolved to dispatch again with a missive and one hundred picols of pepper, keloera dorpa watrana [uncertain: local place or product name] in embassy to your Honors, which we have not wished to neglect, sending our letters herewith, all the more since his Highness has requested us to write and present both the one and the other to your Honors, namely: That the Company has now for about three years in succession not paid the toll on the transported pepper which according to contract should be paid in cash, therefore it is requested in the most friendly manner that in the future Spanish money be sent for the payment of this, and although we have answered several times that if the scarcity of this coast (in view of the fact that such currency has come little from the fatherland for some time) does not cause this, your Honors would undoubtedly have sent us the same long ago, since the Company is not accustomed to lending for long, therefore his Highness still requests patience, as there is otherwise a sufficient good assortment of cloth in abundance in the warehouse, of which there have been some cases of taking, but received in the end again word that the Company according to contract (as said) owes money and not liveries for the exported pepper toll to be paid, and although his Highness still stands debit with 8771 reals (besides the recently sent pieces of cannon and gunpowder), (to settle which he makes no effort at all), he nevertheless remains equally unwilling to pay the aforementioned toll.

text_translated_detailed: Therefore, (Honorable gentlemen), it will be highly necessary that Your Lordships write to His Highness that no one may trade or travel there without Your Lordships' obtained license and passports, for such has never been done without prohibition being taken from here. The principal settlement of the Lampongs, after some days of siege, they (after the enemy had already abandoned it beforehand) have dispersed, and offered it to the red [uncertain: possibly a ritual or ceremonial act], over which from that region victory was fought to be heard again, with some rebellious villages still remaining in the Riesaemh [uncertain: possibly a region or administrative division] to be brought [under control], four Commerijn [uncertain: possibly a place or administrative unit] situated [there], how it will proceed there time will tell. Besides this goes a small request for some Spanish cash money, medicines, provisions for the Comptoir [expanded: trading post], which we humbly request may be sent in the future. This shall be delivered to Your Lordships by the King's second envoy Keloera Patra Watjana [uncertain: proper name], going alongside the letter from His Highness with a gift of 100 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 6,000 kg] of pepper, 6 pieces of elephant tusks, and two pieces [of uncertain commodity]. Signed: Melchior Hurdt, Cornelis Wicxdorp, and Claes Jansz Swart. On the side was written: At the Comptoir [expanded: trading post] — Palembang [Palembang], this 25th of April 1667.

text_translated_detailed: To the Honorable Governor-General and the Honorable gentlemen counselors of India. — Honorable, greatly esteemed, most generous and highly commanding gentlemen, My gentlemen. After we have today, God be praised, safely arrived near Palembang's river, we observed the ship the Meiboom [Meiboom: literally "May Tree"] lying anchored there. Since the violent current turned it back until better tide and wind, so that the same could be advantageous, and since in the night little had passed, we did, upon becoming aware with the lowering of the sail, hear diverse cannon shots to make known their need and to request some fresh water. Wherefore the skipper expressly came to our board and had us allow the same a little to help them out of their water need. Thus they declared themselves very distressed on account of this. Therefore, we had to pass by the command of Your Lordships, requesting over this that Your Lordships not interpret this matter badly, as we had to prefer one necessity over another. Herewith ending, I remain under Your Lordships' great esteemed and most generous commanding gentlemen, in the protection of the Almighty God, [your] servant, and was signed: Isbrandt Vissers. On the side was written: In the yacht the Pauw [Pauw: literally "Peacock"], the 17th of May, Year 1668. — To the Honorable Governor-General and the Honorable gentlemen counselors of India. — Honorable, greatly esteemed, most generous and highly commanding gentlemen, My gentlemen. text_translated_detailed: Therefore we can no longer obtain anything from the Chinese, and likewise we have requested a ship to unload a ship from the pepper warehouse, which today lies loaded with 589,000 cattis [modern equivalent: approximately 350 metric tons] of spices, and we must attend to repairing the damaged plank flooring. The peace struck between the King of England and the High and Mighty States General has been made known here through the dispatch of the proclamation, may the Almighty grant that the same may be maintained for many years to the welfare of both lands and inhabitants. Regarding the renewed war between the Esteemed Company and the Macassarese, the people of this land have not been a little pleased among themselves, just as the King himself, when speaking with our interpreter at court, could not refrain from saying mockingly that the Company could well have spared the gunpowder, pitch barrels, and such things both in Batavia and elsewhere, thereby making it known that it was not yet entirely won. However, afterwards, wishing to soften such matters somewhat, he followed up by saying that the Netherlanders are too good and allow themselves to be led too easily by the nose; they were too easily deceived, etc. May the great God will that the Esteemed Company proceed further against that treacherous nation and other enemies to the terror of the feigned friends with victorious success, amen. With this, noble, earnest, highly esteemed, valiant, wise, prudent, and strict gentlemen, we commend your noble selves to the guidance of the Almighty and, remaining with our humble respects, always your noble gentlemen's obedient servants. And it was signed Melchior Hurdt, Cornelis Wixdorp, Claes Jansz Swardt. At the side it stood: Palembang, at the Comptoir, this 6th of July 1668.

text_translated_detailed: To the Honorable, Esteemed Lord Joan Maetsuycker, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of India, Your Honorable Excellencies, Earnest, Valiant, Your Honorable Excellencies, Well, Wise, Foreseeing, and most Generous Lords, Our well-commanding Lords— Following the departure of our latest writings by the Junk New-Japara dated the 12th of November, on the 9th of December, at the end of the old year, there came to us yet one last opportunity to send Your Honorable Excellency a small advisory letter by certain Malay vessels from here, and copies of both of these now go again herewith. In the writings of the 12th of November, Your Honorable Excellency was made known among other things our taken resolution regarding the under-merchant Sir Johannes van Oppijnen to send him for a time to Indragiri, together with the motives or reasons why, and in the advisory letter of the 9th of December aforementioned, the progress of the said resolution, as well as the speedy departure and safe arrival of the said van Oppijnen in the river of Indragiri, how he, having completed the work, found things there. Item, the further transactions carried out there, we shall not relate at length in this letter, but shall conduct ourselves in this matter by the written report delivered to us by him, said van Oppijnen, on the 24th of the past month upon his return from Indragiri to Jambi, and a copy of which goes herewith, and to which we shall conduct ourselves, in the approval of Your Honorable Excellency, with all humility. Submitted by the Esteemed Willem Volger and the council aforementioned to their Honour on the 7th and 8th of April 1668. His Highness, thus warned, came to the Pangeran at once, together with Keij Ranga and well 200 men, with one vessel to water, laying the mentioned prau alongside, unloading from it all that was found therein. And they brought it into the Pangeran's house. His Highness himself came to our lodge at the last watch of midnight, knocked, and being let in, recounted all that he had done. In the morning, 4 of the same would come so that our smith with his equipment could open the pepper itself, the seized chests and counting houses, in order to examine them. We excused this politely and advised His Highness that he could much better demand the keys from the English themselves, and tell them thereby that if they did not give them, he would have everything that was under lock broken open. This advice was followed, and the keys, which were sent for, were handed over. Upon examination, in 4 counting houses nothing else was found than papers, 12 taels [modern equivalent: approximately 450 grams] of black land gold, and 115 reales [modern equivalent: Spanish silver coins] in cash. In the chests, two of the chief, Mr. Meijnstont, one of the second persons, and then still one of the assistant, Herwijer, there was nothing other than all manner of clothing, necessary for a human body. Now it stands here upon their request for forgiveness of their flight, that their aforesaid goods will be returned to them, which, however, has not yet occurred. His Highness Pangeran de Pattij was yesterday early (that nothing bad happened) in our lodge and has given us by word of mouth and charged us to send to Your Excellencies a certain list of demands, accompanying this letter. Your Excellencies will be pleased to see thereby how unlimited this prince goes in the same. We will not say anything to it, but Your Excellencies' wisdom will examine it. In our judgment, it exceeds, particularly regarding Johor. Keij Ranga sent and presented to His Highness Excellency the Lord Governor-General 6 pieces (as he says, exquisite Fambyse rottings, 3 pieces with silver fittings, and 3 likewise without fittings)—and Keij de Mang 2 pieces of white pepper. From Pangeran de Pattij blasts all his cannons. Pangeran Diepa likewise, and ours do the same. So Pangeran Ratou sent 10 picols of pepper as a gift. Letter from Keij Ranga. Item, his brother's son, Keij de Mang Souria Negara, 2 picols of white pepper, which he says he will hand over to us. Yesterday, at the departure of Keij de Mang Aria Wangsa, first ambassador from here to Your Excellencies (the second will be Keij de Mang Wiera Marta, and Juda Prana the third in the same commission, to follow next Monday), Pangeran de Pattij had all his cannons, both on the land side as well as the water side, fired off brightly. text_translated_detailed: His Highness charged us to write to Your Excellencies that he did this—outside of custom now—out of respect for the good news from our beloved fatherland. We have not remained silent on this action either, but have caused the Esteemed Company to fire 50 pounds of gunpowder in return. So immediately, upon the closing of this letter, we received overland from Palembang a missive from the merchant Sir Melchior Hurdt, chief there, dated the 24th of last month, which we have deemed good to have copied in haste and to append herewith, in order that Your Excellencies may see what in that region passes both in war as in embassies. Wherewith, Esteemed, earnest, highly honorable, manly, wise, provident, and generous lords, &c. My Esteemed lords, Your Excellencies' ever faithful and dutiful servants remain, and was signed Wilhelm Volger, J. v. Oppijnen. To the side stood Jambi. In the Comptoir of the Council, the 7th of April 1668. Still lower stood: Your Highness Excellencies' lords. After the closing of this letter, we understood from Keij de Mang Souria Myara that Pangeran Ratou will have 10 picols of pepper handed over to us, serving from His Highness as a gift to Your Highness Excellencies. Item, so after the closing, there was sent to us by Keij Hanga a letter which His Excellency writes to Your Excellencies and has requested us to append, together with the rottings of which mention was made above, which is now done.

text_translated_detailed: Further request from Pangeran de Pattij regarding his requested assistance against Johor, proposal from the Honorable Willem Volger to remove the English from Jambi. To Batavia, to the Honorable Mister Joan Maatzugker, Governor-General, and the Honorable Gentlemen of the Council of India. Together with His Honorable Excellency and our well-commanding lords, by the Honorable Willem Volger and the Council, sent to their Honorable Excellencies on the 8th of April 1668. Just as we yesterday evening closed our papers to your Excellencies, and the Kiai de Mang Naiaria Wangsa, the first envoy, who had been driven away the day before, we had sent downstream, Pangeran de Pattij comes this afternoon toward the end of our divine service, in the lodge, after some preceding discourse, took us both from the other company apart, and said then, that he well could understand that your Excellencies, for his sake, would not wish to begin open war with those of Johor, moreover that he had therefore instructed the aforementioned envoy to inform your Excellencies of the refusal of the first request, but, it was possible to persuade [you] to send two yachts and two chaloupes [small boats] for the Jambi river, and with one of said chaloupes to threaten Johor a little, moreover with Ragia Moeda [uncertain: possibly a title or name] to bring [matters] so far that he would have to resolve to come to Jambi with his wife, and together with Paduca Touwan (who is held here for the cause of all the troubles that have arisen) his father-in-law Pangeran Ratou to seek forgiveness, his Highness was then willing to enter into a new and lasting alliance with Johor and to maintain it, and although we can sufficiently understand that such an undertaking would fall costly upon the Company, and therefore is entirely not suitable, nevertheless we cannot refrain from making this known to your Excellencies in this separate letter thus briefly, and thereupon to show once more, whether now the right time

text_translated_detailed: To the Honorable, Esteemed Lord Joan Maatsuijcker, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords of the Council of India. — Honorable, Esteemed, Earnest, Valiant, Most Worthy, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords, Our Well-Commanding Lords. Since the departure of our last missives, dated the 7th of last month, and a follow-up letter of the 8th of the same, which were sent to your Honorable Excellencies by way of Jambijsen, the sent messenger of the Naiaria Wangsa, little or almost nothing worthy of writing has occurred here. text_translated_detailed: Esteemed, the remarkable governance of Jambi shall become clear. The father, who otherwise in all matters that occur conducts himself throughout and acts as if he had not even placed his son in the position of Patih, and authorized him to act with his own authority in that regard, complains here that his aforementioned son undertook the dispatch to Your Honorable Excellency without even asking him for counsel or his advice. We regard this entire matter, however, as nothing more than a loose trick of his Highness's aforementioned scheming, practiced solely so that if his son's request as Patih is rejected by Your Honorable Excellency, he can then claim to be ignorant and to have nothing to do with the matter. What befell us on the 26th and the two days following thereof of the aforementioned month, with various boats of his Highness's retinue, concerning some 400 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 24,000 kg] of pepper, which he obtained from the uplands, we shall likewise not relate at length, but in order to save time, we must point Your Honorable Excellency (with all due respect) to the aforementioned extract of the daily register, where everything is set forth at length and as it occurred. Your Excellency will be pleased to see thereby how and what practices his Highness seeks to bring into play in order to raise the pepper price from 4 reals [modern equivalent: a monetary unit] per picol in time back to 5 reals per picol. We are fully resolved not to meet him in this matter in the slightest degree without special order from Your Honorable Excellency, but to let everything take its course, for if we were to give his Highness such foothold, it would thereafter be held and turned against us. All men, first and foremost Pangeran the Patih, and then furthermore each one without exception, we hope, Your Honorable Excellency will judge this as good and well-considered. text_translated_detailed: To the Honorable Lord Joan Maetsuyker, No. Governor General, and the Honorable Lords Councillors of India — Honorable, Esteemed, Courageous, Most Respectable, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords, Our Well-Commanding Lords. On the 15th of this month, we had prepared a small advisory letter to Your Honorable Excellency, and the same, together with an extract from our daily register, under cover of S. R. Ockersen, placed in the hands of a Bantenese Javanese (who, coming here, had brought us a letter from D. O. S. R. Ockersen from there), with the assurance that he would depart the following day; however, this did not happen, but the aforementioned prau [small sailing vessel] was held up by Pangeran Diapa Negara until now, and since the English intend to dispatch the prau, which came here six days ago for their account from Bantam, back there again this evening, we have deemed it good to withdraw our aforementioned advisory letter and, joining it with this second advisory, to send it to Your Honorable Excellency with the skipper of the said prau (who has likewise handed us a small letter from S. R. Ockersen) under cover as above, so that Your Honorable Excellency may thereby come to understand how and in what manner Pangeran Ratou Tragte attempted to raise the price of pepper again from 4 [reals] to 5 reals, and what we had done against this; the matter stands with the same at present still as before. The peace with England will, without doubt, cause His Highness to hold it even more firmly, just as we have reason to see, or seem to perceive, that private merchants are also thinking of this, who, instead of bringing their pepper to the Company's warehouse, are now beginning to store it in their own houses. Among others, a certain Kienije Reridouta, this one being the greatest pepper merchant of all Jambi, we are assured, has already nearly a thousand picols [modern equivalent: approximately 60,000 kilograms] in stock within Jambi.

text_translated_detailed: April 1668. Extract from the Jambi daily register concerning what transpired and was agreed upon between Pangeran Ratou, the East Indian Company's old resident, and the residents of the Honorable Company. On Tuesday the 24th of the same month, the pepper that was received yesterday was, this day before and after noon, purified by the mill and harp of its filth (which was particularly considerable from the English party), so Pangeran Ratou found it good, and being already evening, decided to go visit him, which indeed happened, for when we arrived at his house we were immediately brought inside and before the sleeping chamber of His Highness, where we found Pangeran Proba Negara and Kieij Damang Souria Negara, along with several other gentlemen and many women. His Highness had us come close to his bed and sit down. He spoke very softly and asked us what his son Pangeran de Patij had requested from Batavia and from Your Honors and Excellencies the Governor-General and the Council of India. We, considering this question more as mere curiosity than anything else, answered therefore (as was also true) that we had not seen the aforementioned letter, much less heard it read, but we had heard from His Highness's Patij orally that he wished to request two yachts and two chaloups [chaloups: small sailing vessels]. His Highness then showed himself displeased with this, protested, and took us as witnesses that all of this had happened without his knowledge, and further asked whether, in our opinion, Your Honors and Excellencies would also be inclined to grant such a request. We answered that time would be the teacher in that matter, since it was impossible for us to know, much less to say what Your Honors and Excellencies' thoughts and resolutions would be regarding this matter. With such discourse the time passed until the falling of evening, when he stood up reminding us to request permission

text_translated_detailed: Kieij Demangh came to us with a request, and we were not unwilling to accept the pepper, of which there was discussion yesterday, at 5 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] per picol [modern equivalent: unit of weight, approximately 62.5 kg], on account of the feared consequences. His Excellency said we need not be concerned about this in the least, since it would be possible for His Highness to keep it secret in his own heart and would not make it known to any person in the world, along with a hundred similar reasons and arguments, all tending toward the goal of driving us to the rope, so to speak, and if possible, to ensnare us. And although we were fully resolved not to agree to anything in this matter for any reason whatsoever, we nevertheless requested to be relieved of Kieij Demangh's difficult insistence, asking for time to consider the matter, with the assurance that we would make our thoughts on this matter known more fully and completely to Kieij Ranga tomorrow, so that it could be conveyed by His Excellency to His Highness, the aforementioned Ratou. Kieij Demangh, seeing that there was nothing to say against this answer, held his peace, or showed himself satisfied with it, and departed, as it seemed, well content, to his house. This is, in short, what transpired on this day. Saturday the 28th of the same month, being occupied in the morning with the receipt of 321 picols of pepper, Kieij Ranga came to us early at the lodge to obtain our resolution on the matter and the answer we had given yesterday to Kieij Demangh Souria Negara. Hereupon there fell again many and various discussions, which I shall pass over and omit in order to spare time and paper. The conclusion was that Kieij Ranga would go to Pangeran Ratou and request His Highness on our behalf that he would be pleased to desist from his desire of the 7th of April 1668, which was recounted at length; if so, we would and should come to thank His Highness with an extraordinary gift, at Kieij Ranga's discretion.

Word came that His Highness had rejected this condition and had said that if we did not wish to accept his pepper at 5 rixdollars per picol, he would send it to Betchin [modern equivalent: Batavia/Jakarta] or elsewhere, where it could fetch a higher price. This is, in summary, what we have encountered with Pangeran Ratou and his pepper over three days, and also a sign that this old miser is not yet ready to be swept away. We, however, are and remain determined to let this entire matter take its course and to wait and see what will come of it.

text_translated_detailed: May, Year 1668. Extract from the Jambi daily register, concerning a serious attack by a party, as well as others, without one being able to know why, on the 24th of May, Year 1668, carried out on the lodge, and the little that Pangeran did in the matter of administering proper punishment therefor in the following days. Sunday the 24th of the same month. Early in the morning, the English received by express prau [modern equivalent: type of boat] the letters from their agent at Bantam [modern equivalent: Banten], by which they were advised that the peace between the Crown of England and the United Netherlands had been concluded on the 21st old style, or 31st of July new style [modern equivalent: calendar systems] of the past year, within Breda [modern equivalent: city in the Netherlands], without their being able to say anything else about it. The chief, Mr. Maijnstom (as I was told), cried out with joy when the letter was opened and read, and likewise showed his joy with much shooting. Around 9 o'clock, or half past nine, as I was sitting in my chamber with some merchants who had appeared to weigh their pepper, and talking, waiting for Mr. van Oppijnen, there came about 9 or 10 Bugis [modern equivalent: ethnic group from Sulawesi] with bare creeses [modern equivalent: type of dagger] and other drawn weapons, and with a most fearful screaming, they sprang through the gate to the steps of the lodge, positioning themselves with terrible fury, as if they wanted to kill and murder everything that came before them (like right madmen), but seeing the door of the lodge hastily shut, they held themselves at the place that lies between the gate and the door of the lodge, jumping and screaming like mad and furious men. An inhabitant of the Company's lodge (named Pasquael Morelo) hearing the commotion, came running with shield and sword, as did also a slave of the Company. These two persons were attacked by the aforementioned violent men in the most cruel and furious manner, so that we thought both of them would be struck down there immediately.

In Jambi, upon the arrival of many troublemakers, and likewise what had befallen them with the same, and so forth. This was recounted to Kieij Ranga by the slaves themselves, namely that some of them, through threats with drawn krises [curved daggers] and various fist blows, had chosen the water, and others had fled through the gate in order to save their lives in this way. To the Honored Excellency Mister Joan Maetzuijker [Joan Maetsuyker], Governor General, and the Honored Gentlemen Councilors of India: Honored Excellency, Earnest, valiant, great, esteemed, wise, foreseeing, and very generous. Our well-commanding Lords. Your Honored Excellency's very pleasant letters dated the 26th of May and 9th of June last have reached us, the first by the Junk Japara, and the other by the ship, the Junk Japara and sailing son, on the 6th and 15th of the past month, respectively, and it was pleasing to us at first to see that our letters successively written from here to Your Honored Excellency and sent with various opportunities were also properly delivered. We hope that from our most recent advisory letter of the 30th of May last, together with an extract from our Day Register by way of Bantam, covered by Sir Ockersz, Your Honored Excellency will learn of this. However, if the delivery of the same had not been followed through (although we have no reason to doubt it), it is deemed worthy of effort by us to attach herewith copies of both the said advisory letter and the Extract of the Day Register, so that Your Honored Excellency might then be able to and be pleased to observe how everything stood at that time here. Since then, there has been little or indeed no change in it, nor in other matters either. Therefore, we shall endeavor, with due respect and in all humility, to answer the following to Your Honored Excellency's two very pleasant letters mentioned above.

Among other things, we have made known to Your Honored Excellency in our aforementioned most recent advisory from here how a certain Langpasser (chief of the Jambi robbers, who increase daily) had encountered, attacked, and seized a certain vessel, said to come from Achin north of Indragiri, with the result that the same is seen daily with the booty. Indeed, he also appeared here at the beginning of the past month. The owners of the aforementioned vessel, being mostly Javanese from the East, and some Borneese, Pangeran Ratou (under whom the said Langpasser is subordinate) has declared all of them free, but regarding the full restitution of their goods, people shrug their shoulders, as many of them have been lost. We shall leave this here and ride once on a horse that trots somewhat harder. The mentioned robber, on his return from the north, encountered directly before the river of Indragiri a vessel coming from Malacca manned with 17 or 18 Coppens [crew members], and some assure us that among them were 2 white persons. The owners of the aforementioned vessel, being mostly Javanese from the East, and some Borneese, Pangeran Ratou (under whom the said Langpasser is subordinate) has declared all of them free, but regarding the full restitution of their goods, people shrug their shoulders, as many of them have been lost. text_translated_detailed:
To the Honorable, Esteemed, Most Wise and Generous Gentlemen, the Governor-General Joan Maatsuiker and the Esteemed Council of the Indies at Batavia [Jakarta], our well-commanding Lords.

With the present occasion that English friends are dispatching an express vessel from here to Bantam, we have likewise not dared or been able to refrain from serving your Honorable Excellency by this route with a letter of advice, and moreover, or rather through an extract from our day register (since the departure of the aforementioned vessel only came to our attention yesterday, and we were occupied for most of that entire day by Sangerman Ratou), to make briefly known the state of the Esteemed Company's affairs here, and among other things to show what the household of Pangeran de Patij has maintained with us since the departure of the yacht the Sun, dated the 12th of this month, with our writings of the 9th thereof, and a cargo of pepper from here to the coast, we have not doubted that your Honorable Excellency will find, in reading the aforementioned extract from the day register, various troubling matters; but none among them that have not been properly settled by us on the civil account. It seemed that with the return or again the return of the 78 Jambian envoys from Batavia here, and the receipt of your Honorable Excellency's missive, which was on the 15th of last month, his Highness might have had a change of heart and would have conducted himself somewhat more carefully thereafter, although we have until now perceived little or almost no improvement. The reading of your Excellency's Honorable missive, in which his Highness's words were mentioned, caused first of all great alteration and much deliberation in appearance, and nothing else as if one wished to begin immediately to demand and collect the Company's heavy outstanding debts with force, but what has followed from it? Not the least effect thereof.

text_translated_detailed: Eight days to remain, we wished to observe the opening of the packages to see if perhaps another of the same assortment might slip through, and upon discovery, his highness would then send the same home, and so forth—this more as a proper presentation, as it had been offered beyond our means, was nevertheless not accepted by his highness, but the same requested that we should immediately go into the warehouse and from package to package and with an open eye of the same examine and search. Or if another package of the same small roses slipped through and could be found, yet noticing that we remained standing with all courtesy at our first excuses, he came with an angry head and left the lodge without speaking a word. We gave his highness the customary honor of escort and shooting, although without acknowledgment—his highness was troubled—about a quarter hour outside the lodge, or the basin was overturned, and likewise all and each inhabitant of Jambi [Jambij] was thereby forbidden to receive any clothes from our lodge or to carry them outside the gate thereof, upon forfeiture of the same clothes, and moreover according to the circumstances of the persons, to incur a monetary fine. His answer was that we should lay our head in the lap, and although we had no guilt (which he himself had to admit), yet we must ask pardon, and thus satisfy the pangeran. We asked further on what grounds such a thing should happen, for to have no guilt and to confess guilt, we considered to be two contrary things, which therefore ought not to be requested by people of knowledge from people of knowledge, unless one was out to make both the pangeran and us a laughingstock before the world, and so forth. But since Kjeij Maes said that if we could bring it about with his highness that the pretended pardon remained behind, and yet with a reversal the selling of our clothes was opened and published, then we would, a day or two thereafter, come to thank his highness with a considerable gift.

In Jambi, September 1668. text_translated_detailed: We presented to His Highness a gift worth approximately 50 rixdollars [modern equivalent: a substantial sum], which he refused, saying that he could not accept it at present, since he had come here solely to go fishing. We then requested that His Highness not disdain this meager gift of ours (since it was the first time that His Highness had come to the lodge during our tenure), but he persisted in his refusal, so that after some further complimentary protests the gift was taken away again. With this His Highness departed again with the evening, the fishing having turned out even better than we had expected, since we could not imagine otherwise than that it was aimed at our vessels. — On this day, due to the arrival of the necessary equipment for shipping tomorrow not being able to be brought together, we were forced to postpone it until the day after tomorrow. — Wednesday the 19th of the same month we prepared everything that was necessary for the shipment against the following morning, for which it served us very well that we were not overlooked or troubled by anyone that day. Thursday the 20th of the same month, although the sabandars arrived fairly late in the day, we nevertheless pressed the work forward in such a way that we finished weighing the pepper in the evening, but we had to leave approximately 400 sacks lying in the place of the lodge due to the approaching night, which were then properly covered with matting [cadjang: a type of woven mat] and guarded by the people of the sabandar, out of fear that we might have wanted to and been able to increase this shipment during the night—see how suspicious our loyalty is here. Friday the 21st of the same month, the remaining pepper that we had been forced to leave in our place yesterday, having been shipped today, we then made everything ready for the Junk [ship name] N.t Japara and the small boat to be sent adrift early tomorrow morning.
