text_translated_detailed: To the High Excellencies, Mister Joan Maetsuijcker, Governor General, and the Noble gentlemen counselors of India. — Jambi. Most Esteemed, Valiant, Great, Honorable, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Gentlemen, — Our well-commanding gentlemen. On the first of this month we recently had the occasion to send to your High Excellencies by way of Bantam a small vessel, expressly sent by the English friends from here, with a small letter and an extract from our daily register, all brief according to the circumstances of the time, to serve. What your High Excellencies were made aware of thereby will (if necessary) the copy enclosed herewith be able to show. It was not without reason that we complained in the said writings as much about Pangeran Depati as about his father Ratou, for the first has done us various gross wrongs from time to time and continues still in his unbearable actions, and the other, namely Pangeran Ratou, demands from us or to speak more correctly from your High Excellencies 4 to 500 reals which the brother of Chinte— had lost at Batavia here. Item, in place of the fact that his Highness should have been pleased with your High Excellencies' order regarding the aforementioned 200 piculs of pepper, which your High Excellencies charged us to write off to his Highness's account as a reduction of his greater debts and to make good, he forgot us and demanded from us the price of Batavia for it, that is Rials 6 per picul [modern equivalent: approximately 6 reals per picul]. Despite all this, his Highness dared to lay before us and command us to write to your High Excellencies regarding their alleged damage on the west coast and in the strait of Malacca (so they claim), estimating the same at Reals 5,117, together with their desire to equalize and settle the same, both against his Highness as well as the debt of Kiai Demang Souria Negarate.

text_translated_detailed: On the 12th of July, in the year 1668, in the fluyt [a type of Dutch merchant ship] the Zantlooper from Batavia to Biliton and Banca, a daily record kept by the Under-Merchant Jan de Harde of what occurred on his voyage from Batavia to the islands of Banca and Biliton and what was reported there on the spot, having been sent there by His Excellency the Governor-General Joan Maetzuijker and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies with the fluyt the Zantlooper in company with Raja Banca. Thursday morning we set sail together from Batavia's roadstead, meanwhile I sent the small boat the Fortuin to the vessel of Raja Banca with respectful request that His Excellency would be pleased to come aboard our ship to receive the gift from His Esteemed Excellency the General, whereupon he immediately came aboard with his own vessel, and it seemed he was very pleasant to speak with, which was agreeable to me. I welcomed His Excellency and gave him the aforementioned gift consisting of 3 bolts of red cloth, 12 bolts of passement [a type of trim or braid], and 2 pairs of embroidered slippers, which I respectfully presented to him in the cabin in the name of His Excellency. His Excellency accepted the same with gratitude and further requested to be able to enjoy for the journey 100 pounds of gunpowder, 16 muskets, 300 dozen bullets, 2 bandoliers and a bundle of straw, with which he was accommodated. He then promised us that he would always remain with us on the journey, and because we would not be able to find each other while sailing at night or in bad weather, I deemed it good that we, as long as we are sailing at night, should light one fire, but when at anchor, two dozen from our ship, for his guidance. He earnestly requested and desired that we sail with him in company first to the island of Biliton where he was residing, both to visit his wife and child and to trade with the great ones there,

text_translated_detailed: signed J. de Harde, Baltus Groen, Philips de Bricquenij, Willem Willems Vermij, Abe Gerbrants, and Abraham van Burgh. July, Anno 1668. In the fluyt the Zantloper by the east shore of Billiton, in the evening around half past eight, we weighed anchor and went under sail. Shortly thereafter we encountered a hard squall of rain and wind, and tacked even in the moonlight (although that was not wise), above the east point of the island, between and beside various shallows and reefs, indeed at times no more than a ship's length away from them in water of only two and a half fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 15 feet], which lasted until two o'clock after midnight before the skipper let the anchor fall to the bottom, to my great relief. July 26th. Thursday morning early we found ourselves surrounded by shallows as if besieged, and we could not help but marvel greatly at how we escaped without any damage, for which the great God must be believed and thanked. Shortly thereafter, while we were busy weighing anchor, the cable rope broke into pieces and our anchor, weighing about fifty pounds, slipped backward. When we came to anchor again, we could not sail further because of the shallows. Friday, in the afternoon, the weather improving somewhat, we sent our sloop on the 27th of this month close under the shore to sound the depth of the water along the coast above the point lying ahead and to see if the ship could pass through it. But when some people came to speak, we first asked about Raja Banca or otherwise called Padalong, to inquire where he keeps his dwelling place on this island and to have him return to us as quickly as possible. July 28th. Friday: in the afternoon the sloop returned to our ship and on Saturday we anchored. The cartographer informed us that ahead, above the three nearest islands, it is three to four fathoms deep and the ship can sail through it well. Behind the largest of the islands we perceived several fishermen's vessels with women and children in them, and speaking with them we learned that there are some small rivers along here, but that Padalong, as mentioned before, beyond the first point to the south of them, has his residence within a very large river. Upon this we made ready to go under sail, but as soon as we thought to lift the anchor from the bottom, the cable rope broke into pieces again. However, after much effort we finally recovered it, and being of the intention to go under sail in the morning, God the Lord willing, with good weather and wind, may the Company be preserved from such or similar damage. So Champrou had sent to Batavia to request assistance against their enemies on Billiton, in such a way that the Company would henceforth take them under their protection and defense, recognize them, and obey them. He said it was because Kiagaria sought to kill him, after he, on the order of the Pangeran of Palembang, had let his father, the ruling Tommegong, be killed by kris dagger without guilt. And such affronts and insults of the past were so great and the eternal shame not to be forgiven nor forgotten, and they were not to endure the other named Pangeran of Palembang any longer. So Champrou had sent to Batavia to request assistance against their enemies on Billiton, in such a way that the Company would henceforth take them under their protection and defense, recognize them, and obey them. But the aforementioned Champrou is not here as a raja nor as a land governor of Billiton, but rather as a co-ruler on Banca, having been driven out by what is His Excellency of Palembang, and is now married and dwelling in the river Coubou, confirmed also by those who drew here and those who went again from here to other places.

Furthermore, the aforementioned Samprou (whose residence is always in the mangrove swamps of Toubou, as he was driven out from Palembang from the island of Banca, and has now placed himself under the aforementioned panglima) was a man of great standing and lineage among the Bancanese, and they also, being willing to accept him as their lord, would accept and obey him as their lord and king, if the Company would protect and defend them here on the aforementioned island against all their enemies. For which reason (in hope of obtaining Billiton under his control), he has presented himself to His Excellency in Batavia as Raja or lantvoogt [regional administrator] of both the aforementioned islands. But he said with high words that I should not doubt the good success of the contract made between the Company and the aforementioned Samprou, wishing with his wife and children that it would prosper. Here it now appears and will be further confirmed that the aforementioned Samprou is not recognized by the subjects of both kingdoms of the aforementioned islands as a legitimate lord or sovereign ruler, and how the matter will further develop on Banca, I hope to see confirmed with our arrival there. Although nevertheless, according to the circumstances learned from various discourse and my own observation here at this place, I cannot judge otherwise or have [uncertain: original text] in Batavia (under correction) regarding his person been entirely abused, and whoever learns the cause from time. After midday, around 4 o'clock, I took my leave and went back from land and arrived around half past five with the Chaloupe on board. Sunday celebrated. But I then learned that His Excellency had gone to his dwelling place Coubou, which lies nearby here, to bring his wife and child here, and to let them depart as he comes, under notice of the panglima. He is expected to return again at the latest. The island has since become completely desolate and wild, and they have also been forced to purchase various necessities of life, namely rice, salt, sugar, onions, and garlic, and so forth, which they would not have needed to buy if the inhabitants could have supplied themselves and brought them from other places. They wished to be able to live once more as peacefully and quietly as in the time of their deceased Pangiran Ourata mentioned before. They would then be able to cultivate the land, which is good and fertile, in such a manner that they would not need anything of the aforementioned necessities except for coarse cloth and linen from other places. In return, he had offered them iron, wash [uncertain: original term], and dams for unloading, up to two or three of the common Javanese vessels, and that within the time of four or five months.

text_translated_detailed: Lords of the Council of India here commissioned for this purpose, to have further proof and certainty of the request made by the aforementioned Raja Sampou on the one hand, and the aforementioned honored rulers on the other hand, after some conferences held, a further mutual bond and alliance has been made and established in the manner as follows. First, the Governor-General and the Council promise on their side to take the aforementioned rulers with their aforementioned island and people under the protection and safeguard of the Company in August of the year 1668, in the small vessel the Zantloper before Coloon, and to hold them under the protection and safeguard of the Company against all enemies who shall wish to offend them or their subjects or do them wrong in any manner as is set forth in the aforementioned document. In return, the aforementioned rulers, on their side, for themselves and their successor rulers of the aforementioned island, promise and undertake to hold and recognize the aforementioned Company from now on as their rightful protector and lord as long as the sun and moon shall shine in the heavens, and to remain faithful and loyal to them as such closely allied ones befit. It is therefore that he shall likewise admit no other nation or people into the land to trade or dwell there except the subjects of the aforementioned Company or those to whom the same shall grant permission and allow. Furthermore, the aforementioned rulers also promise to the aforementioned Company for their undertaken protection an annual honorable recognition to be brought from the fruits which the land produces. Thus done and contracted at the east side of Banca at the river Coloor, and the contracting parties, in knowledge of the truth, have confirmed this with their respective signatures on the 25th of August of the year 1668. text_translated_detailed: It will be possible to go to Batavia with speed to bring His Excellency news from one end and the other. text_translated_detailed: in the bay of Quala Banca we came to anchor. I went with the prau to land, which our people had done before, and had spoken with some people, but there was no one on the shore. Meanwhile, beside a certain small stream we found a good path, and we went along it inland through forests and at times through long grass for about an hour and a half, until we came close to some mountains, both large and small. There we heard various people speaking, but saw none. But since evening overtook us, and we were only five strong and not well provided with weapons, we sought the same path back, and came completely dark to the shore by our prau, which also went back to the ship. We are nevertheless of the intention, if God permits, to resume the same tomorrow morning so that we might know what kind of settlement or village it is, as well as how the land is situated. The 6th of the same, Thursday, early in the morning, according to intention, going inland with our persons, 4 men came to meet us, having some riders, potatoes, and such with them to exchange the same with our people on the shore for cloth and cash. They then returned and brought us to their village or settlement called Parmissan, situated about 2 hours' walk from our location, behind and at a large mountain where a stream of fresh water runs between both. The settlement was round about surrounded by 3 thick and high palisades [palisades: wooden fortifications], standing well 2 feet apart from each other, and within there were well 25 or 30 atap [atap: palm-thatched] houses inhabited by about 80 people, men, women, and children. September of the year 1668. In the fluyt the Zantlooper before Quala Banca, 93. Also with some clove trees, coconut palms, banana, and durian trees planted, and furthermore we saw that around there was nothing else.

text_translated_detailed: At one o'clock we came to our people, who were fetching fresh water, and the skipper also came there. After we had eaten something and our boat and small vessel [Chialoep] had taken on water supplies, we went with the others toward evening back to the ship on the 7th of the same month, Friday. Around 11 o'clock I went with the fresh water in our small vessel [Chialoep] to the aforementioned river called Quala Banca, and arrived there late in the evening around half past nine with the tide at both settlements, where we let our anchor fall, which by estimation was about 5 miles up the river. Meanwhile, two small boats came with some Palembang traders to the small vessel [Chialoep] and asked us what company we came from. I said from Malacca, that we needed some rice, since we had had a long journey, and only to give them no bad suspicion of my arrival and the reason for it. They said that the lord himself was in difficulty regarding this, since in this east monsoon no vessel from the Javanese coast had yet arrived. We further received as an answer to my question that the harbor master named Djagaracxa, who had departed with the ambassador of Palembang to Mataram, held authority here, this place being the main settlement of the entire island of Banca, called Quala Banca, where all the recognition [tribute] from the inhabitants of the land is brought and received through the aforementioned pangivan [official], consisting of some iron, wash [uncertain: original text], and small streams. Met boven geciteerde Iacht overveen is ons mede schrijvens terhant gecomen, van den E: daniel six opperhooft ende den Raadt in Japan, waar uijt wij voor eerst met lieff verstaan hebben 't behouden arrivement van't schip de gerechticheijdt aldaar, als mede hoe zijn aangebrachte coopmanschappen naar in houde der factura gerespondeerte hadden, mitsgaders hoe deselve aldaar een goede marck aangetreffen ende met de gerequireerde winsten vergenegotieert waaren, 't welcke ons dan doet Amimeeren omme op de novo gedaane petitie soo veel hartevellen en koehuijden in te samelen als het Immers doenelijck wesen sal Wij verneemen uijt voorgemelte missive ongaerne hoe de Iammamats ofte Elantshuijden al vrij wat van de worm gegeten en Jappan aan den marckt souden gebragt zijn, dat ons ten hoogsten doet verwonderen vermits de zelve vellen van hier soo gaaf en deugtsaam versonden sijn, als wij verclaaren in eenige Iaaren herwaarts te zijn geschickt, oversulcx wij ons niet anders connen Imagineeren off voor Septemb. Ao. 1684 1 voorseijde vellen moeten in't schip op een zeer vogtige plaatse gelegen hebben, waar door se dit quaat aangecomen zijn, te meer wij op het havenen en Cloppen den selven meer regart doen neemen als oijt voordesen geschiet zij, waaromme ons dan oock noijt eenige Clagten daar van, als alleenlijck nu, toegecomen sijn — voor d'aanstaande negotie van Iapan werden van hier d' naarvolgende coopmanschappen g'eijscht, als te weten, soo veel hartevellen alsen tot een verdragelijcke prijs te bemachtigen zullen zijn, 5: a 6: betv.

However, the Tartars would not admit His Honorable to trade at this time, whereupon the aforementioned gentleman, to the Company's detriment, was compelled to navigate the fully laden ships the Oijevaar, Batavia, and Victoria in haste from Hokkien toward Costing. With the aforementioned yacht Overveen, letters have also come to hand from the Honorable Mister Daniel Six, chief and the Council in Japan, from which we have for the first time with pleasure learned of the safe arrival of the ship the Gerechtigheydt [the Righteousness] there, as well as how his brought merchandise had responded according to the contents of the invoice, and likewise how they had found a good market there and had negotiated the same with the required profits. This causes us to be encouraged to collect as many deer hides and cowhides as shall be possible on the newly made petition. We learn from the aforementioned missive with displeasure how the Jamamats or elk hides have already been eaten quite a bit by worms and brought to market in Japan, which causes us the greatest wonder, since those hides were sent from here in such good and sound condition as we declare to have been shipped hither in some years past. Wherefore we cannot imagine otherwise than that before September of the year 1684 the aforementioned hides must have lain in the ship in a very damp place, whereby they came to this damage. The more so since we pay more regard to the stowing and securing of the same than ever happened before, on account of which we have also never received any complaints thereof, except only now. For the forthcoming trade with Japan, the following merchandise is requested from here, namely, as many deer hides as can be obtained at a reasonable price, 5 to 6 [uncertain: unit of measurement]

text_translated_detailed: to make a journey, which he again humbly requests of Your Excellency, to which he hopes Your Excellency will kindly grant him permission, especially since with the end of this year 1668 only a few months will remain of his contracted time, and also because the Company's affairs here can well be attended to by the under-merchant Jan van den Spijck, and he will rely upon this and Your Excellency's permission in the future will be forthcoming. Just as the yacht Overveen had received its full cargo and lay ready for sailing before the bar of Siam to navigate from here to Cochin [Cochin: modern Kochi, India], we were handed over by Oja Berckelangh two elephants to send as a gift to Your Excellency, namely one from the King and one from His Excellency, the aforementioned beasts having come into our hands so late because His Majesty had departed to the upper regions, for which reason we could not send the same to Your Excellency with this ship, as we would have had to hold the yacht Overveen for a considerable time thereafter, considering that the embarking of the said elephants and the bringing down of the same would consume much time, for which reasons we deemed it good to keep the aforementioned beasts here, to send them to Your Excellency from here at a better opportunity, which in former times has indeed been done in this manner several times, whereby we trust we shall have done well, the more so as we understand the aforementioned yacht Overveen is urgently required at Batavia to be refitted there. We have, on account of the long delay of the aforementioned elephants, already wondered whether some gift from His Majesty would be sent to Your Excellency this year, on account of the gift which Your Excellency recently kindly sent hither for the King, which His Majesty, according to his greedy nature, has not at all been pleased with, because the same differed extraordinarily from the previous gifts sent, inasmuch as it amounted to no more in monetary sum than ½ of the gift previously made, for which reason we then, with Your Excellency's approval, request that the King be treated somewhat more liberally in the future, so that we may retain his good disposition in the execution of the Company's business. Your Excellency's letter recently written to Oja Berckelangh is now answered with this yacht. What sort of person the aforementioned Berckelangh is and how he has been very helpful to the Company in its operations here during his office, we have written to Your Excellency in successive letters previously sent, for which reason this gentleman should be remembered by Your Excellency yearly with a reasonable good gift, for the further Siamese great ones, and it will not be necessary, as was customary before, that any gift be sent hither, because the Company's requests are mostly presented and executed at court here by the said Oja Berckelangh, which gentleman is very well regarded by His Majesty and is of great influence here.—In order to prepare a good cargo for Japan

text_translated_detailed: Your Honors should be pleased to consider a reasonable and good remuneration for the aforementioned annually, for the sake of the great Siamese [Siam] affairs, and it will not be necessary, as was customary in the past, to send any gifts hither, because the Company's requests are mostly presented and accomplished at court here through the said Oja Benkelangh [uncertain: title/name], which gentleman is well regarded by His Majesty and possesses great influence here. — In order to procure good cargo and goods for Japan, and likewise to benefit well from the few saleable Coromandel cloths that still remain at the Siam office and to help them to market with the required profits, as well as to carry out the further service of the General Company as is proper, we shall on our part, according to our duty, apply such diligence and effort in the greatest service of our principal lords as lies within our power and is feasible to accomplish, upon which Your Honors may please to rely, and since we have nothing further to advise Your Honors at present, we shall, through lack of further matter, end and conclude, whereby Your Honors, esteemed, valiant, wise, prudent, and most discreet gentlemen, your Honors' obedient servants commend themselves, and it was signed F. Noogh. Poolvoet, Jan van der Spijk, J. D. Keijser, Nicolaes Sigerijdzez. One said stood, India at the Netherlands Office Siam on the 3rd of February in the year 1668.

text_translated_detailed: inquire somewhat further into this Esteemed one. The Counselor Singlamongh is a man of middle stature, brown, dark and shrewd of countenance, soft of speech yet hasty and quick to anger, and great in his assertions. Correct, neat, and very orderly in his household and in all his doings. Intelligent enough, yet not refined, more cunning than wise. And since such a great statesman has much need thereof, very profit-seeking, eager and unashamed in accepting gifts, as well as that which is characteristic of this nation, seems to be very changeable in his opinions. Although the Esteemed one was found to be much more assured in his conduct than the field commander, which we ourselves found good to treat thus, and first with all courtesy to accommodate ourselves to his humor as much as was possible and fitting, and in many matters to turn our compass according to his. Furthermore we found it good, beyond the designated gifts from Your Excellencies, to throw something more into the pot or into the air, so to speak, and to examine how the same would be received. And so to obtain some assurance in a doubtful matter, when this was attempted with a common chain of blood coral and some small trifles, it was found that the same was not only well received, but that the Esteemed one did not hesitate to have some blood coral requested under the pretext that the first chain still lacked fifty to sixty pieces, which he wished to purchase. The compliments were conducted in the same manner as with the field commander, with the lord ambassador saying he was pleased to see Talauja in good health and to be able to appear before his presence. Furthermore, the Dutch had previously enjoyed many favors from the previous Conbons, and his Excellency hoped to be likewise partaker of his highness's favor. Upon this the Conbon asked whether his Excellency had completed the Peking journey in good health. The Conbon answered that the ambassador had brought the Chinese in Peking, in which the emperor had taken good pleasure. Why then should he not be favorable to the ambassador? After which no further discussion ensued, but we parted in good spirits after some compliments. Year 1667, November 6th and 9th, in Lamthaij, the suburb of Hocksieuw. Meanwhile, Monsieur Putmans had gone to court with a project of the field commander's gift (which had been found good yesterday to present to his highness), but without obtaining an audience, he had to return with orders to come again tomorrow. We had it taken up again the next morning through the Enobel and the aforementioned Monsieur Putmans and also immediately presented it to the Conbon, but our aforementioned friends fared no better than Monsieur Putmans yesterday, and likewise could not obtain an audience from either of them. The project of the field commander's gift having been taken from our aforementioned friends and shown to the Field Commander through the interpreter, the interpreter brought back word that his highness had said he would not accept any gift. Lisiongia said: We have understood that the ambassador has arrived at Lamthaij and request from Talauja that the ambassador will order that the ambassador send a flying messenger below to make the ships depart. Now the field commander says the four Dutch ships departed from here a month and a day ago, and the Haijto and Lisiongia have made this known to the field commander, and the field commander has written a letter about this to the emperor. Now the field commander has again learned from Lisiongia that the ships have come back and want to wait at sea by force for word from the ambassador, and that this is very badly done. Now the field commander orders the Tousies that they shall go at once to the ambassador and have a messenger with a letter go to the ships and that the ships must depart at once, and that he, Hajongtia, and Tousie, shall press the ambassador to send the messenger below and that they shall not cruise outside of that but remain out of sight, so that the Dutch may follow the emperor's order. The lord ambassador gave them the answer that he would let the field commander know.

The understuerman Visbeen and one of the trumpeters (who had been with us above) were ordered by the lord Ambassador to the yacht Blyswijk. His Excellency now requested of these mandarins whether they could go there, upon which they answered that their chests would first have to be inspected. Meanwhile, we had brought down many, indeed about 700 pieces of cloth from above. His Excellency said he had not bought a single piece of cloth and also could not believe that because we had brought so many pieces of cloth with us, they could freely inspect again, placing there (that they had given permission for it) two appointed commissioners.

In Lamthai, the suburb of Boeksiouw, in the year 1667, on the 28th of September, in the evening. In the Gebel, the noble one makes known to the lord ambassador how that he had been in discussion in the afternoon with our neighbor Lappra and a factor from Singlamongh regarding the obtaining of some silk, saying that Lappra would willingly deliver silk to us and have it brought under Tinghaij, if we would leave his Excellency here as a hostage. text_translated_detailed: Journey from Hoeksiuw to Batavia. On the 17th, in the morning with daybreak, we departed with four ships: Victoria, Batavia, Oijeraer, and Bleijswijk from under the disturbed city of Tinghai. We set our course East-South-East and South-East between the little towers and islands, passing close by toward the way, until midnight, when we had passed the island. Then we set course South-West toward the West. In the middle of the dog watch, the wind began to rise greatly, so that we took in the topsails, and in order not to lose sight of the other ships, we struck the foresail to half mast. On the 18th, in the morning, the wind was North-East, blowing a flying storm mixed with rain. We veered with a course somewhat more westerly. The land was a little to the side. We had a depth of 32 to 35 fathoms [vadem] [modern equivalent: approximately 58-64 meters] of muddy sand bottom. In the afternoon it began to clear somewhat. The three other ships were close by us. Toward evening we saw land from West-North-West, and as far as we could tell, it was the island of Quemuy [Quemuij], though we could not obtain certainty through the fog. On the 19th, it was still a stiff breeze. The yachts [Jaghten] Batavia and Bleijswijk had drifted somewhat from us the previous night, which came back to us at midday. We saw on the land which we believed to be the sand dunes. The depths were [Year 1687, on the 19th of December] in the fluyt [fluijt] Victoria sailing from Hoeksiuw toward Batavia, being 20 to 25 fathoms of sand, and thereafter muddy sand bottom. On the 20th, in the morning, the wind was North-East, a moderate breeze. We saw the land and found it to be the Macassar Islands [Maccause Eijlanden]. In the afternoon we set our course South-West toward the island of Aynam [Aijnam], finding that in the three previous days we had advanced 120 miles [mijlen] to the west. Thursday, the 5th of August 1666, before the river Hocksieu. In council gathering, the Esteemed Lord Ambassador having proposed (after invoking God's blessing) how that we, God be thanked, had all equally come around the sand dunes, and as by resolution of the 6th of July it was established that in case the ships of the others should separate, the rendezvous was determined in the bay of Sothia, or whether at present the service of the Esteemed Company with what was required (in case no danger lay therein) with the ships together to run into the Dutch harbor, which was given to the council for consideration, but as the captains of the Tiger and Alphen, likewise also the chief steersman of the Constance made difficulties, in order to run therein because of the unwieldy nature of their ships, so it was unanimously resolved that the ships Alphen, Tiger and Constance (to avoid all difficulties and to prevent as much as possible) shall sail directly toward the bay of Sothia, and the ships Vlaardingen and Bleijswijk by their good maneuverability according to the statement of the captains, and for other considerations toward the Dutch harbor, to be better at the works. Likewise also that the boats and sloops of the ships here on board shall come, to be helpful to the ships in all cases, and if the weather and wind permit such, the ships Alphen, Constance and Tiger shall hold themselves so long before the river until we have knowledge of our arrival in the harbor. Thus done and resolved in the yacht Vlaardingen, sailing before the river Hocksieu on the 5th of August in the year 1666: undersigned and was signed by P. van Hoorn, C. Nobel, D. text_translated_detailed: Corn. Barthelszoon, merchant, Jb. Putmans. — Saturday the 27th of November 1666 — In a meeting, the lord ambassador presented to the council how our merchants Messrs. Nobel and Harthouwer had previously been in conference on several distinct occasions with the factors of the governors regarding our merchandise, and now again today, where the chief factor of the King Singlamong himself had been present, but that these factors, in bidding for pepper, had not come higher than at the narrowest necessity to 10 taels [modern equivalent: unit of weight/currency] per picul [modern equivalent: unit of weight], and for sandalwood 22 taels per picul, on condition that if they paid 10 taels for the picul of pepper, we would then have to accept their raw white silk (according to the sample handed to the aforementioned messrs., which is also very fine) against 200 catties [modern equivalent: unit of weight], and nothing else, saying plainly that in case we did not want to accept their silk, they could then not buy our merchandise, the aforementioned messrs. having exerted all their strength and thought to obtain something more for the pepper and sandalwood than the above-mentioned offer, and for the silk to give something less, but these factors stuck without deviation to their demands and offers, declaring plainly that they could not or would not do otherwise in this matter, and considering that in the instruction granted by the Esteemed lord Governor General and the council of India to the lord ambassador, it is expressly stipulated that in case no shipment with silk from here to Japan could be made this year (which indeed cannot happen now), then the silk may not be purchased higher than against 180 taels per picul, so the lord ambassador asked their advice on what they thought best for us to do in this matter for the greatest service of the Esteemed Company, namely to negotiate for some time longer or

text_translated_detailed: 1686. — In a meeting, the Esteemed lord ambassador, after invoking the name of God's grace, presented to the council how the field commander had let us know yesterday that we must be ready to depart for Peking in 10 days, or whether it would therefore (to give his Highness some satisfaction) not be advisable to make some preparations to be as ready as possible by that time, and that Monsieur Putmans should begin to pack the gift goods firmly according to the memorandum prepared for that purpose by the Esteemed Mr. Nobel and approved by the council, so that he would see that we meant it and it was not lacking on our part: which was thus firmly established. Item, whether one should not provide the people under the retinue of this embassy, against the impending long arduous Peking journey, (at the expense of the Esteemed Company), with clothing and other necessities, against the conditions not a little, which was also deemed necessary since they were very poorly provided with clothing and otherwise, and the secretary of the Doos and steward Ruvenoort were commissioned to investigate how much each person according to their proportion would be needed, and to report this to the ambassador and council, it was also firmly established that Messrs. Nobel and Harthouwer should go today to the house of the Chinese merchant Cisaij to the factors of the governors to ask them seriously whether they wanted to go again as before to the tower to receive pepper or not, and that barges should be sent at once by us to the Tiger at the tower to begin the unloading again, and thus to make their factors understand (because they did not keep their contract regarding the unloading of the pepper) that we were therefore not at a loss, so that they would not take any reflection on it. —

text_translated_detailed: and Harthouwer is conceived to be shown, being necessary to be here somewhat early, or if it should happen that a dispatch might be made to Hangzhou, Ningpo, or some other northern place here in China or indeed to Japan, the Messrs. Harthouwer and Bartels shall be charged, before the arrival of the Batavian ships, to make no dispatch to Japan, in order first to be able to learn the condition of the Japanese trade, but the Batavian ships having come, and some silk being in stock, shall the aforesaid Messrs., deeming it advisable, be able to send the yacht Bleiswijck with yet another vessel, the quantity of silk being considered somewhat, to Japan without waiting for the return of the ambassador, but no Chinese, or their goods, to be allowed to go with the ships thither, so as not to come into conflict with the Japanese. — Furthermore it is deemed good to postpone the unloading of the Constance until the delivered goods shall have been accounted for and paid, and so when the Constance shall be able to depart, as is hoped, its journey shall likewise proceed directly to Batavia, unless other circumstances might come to the fore, as when the greatest service of the Honored Company shall be advanced thereby as with other matters, which shall be done with good deliberation of the Chief Officers Messrs. Harthouwer and Bartels, the under-merchant Frans Limborgh being adjoined thereto as a council member, wherein then the council after the departure of the ambassador here in Xiamen [modern equivalent: Amoy] shall consist. Concerning the Quanzhou matters, the same remain deferred to Messrs. Harthouwer and Bartels, to dispose of them with Bleiswijck or in the return of the Constance in such manner as the service of the Honored Company shall require. — Thus done, resolved, and arrested in Lamtai, the suburb of Xiamen, date as above, undersigned and was signed, Pieter van Hoorn, C. Present His Excellency the lord ambassador Pieter van Hoorn, the Honored Constantin Nobel, and the lord D. Harthouwer, Jan Naelhout, Cornelis Bartelsz, Marchier, Johannes Putmans, and Jol Adriaansz, as assumed members. There appeared in council the fiscal Sir Joan van der Does, together with the captain Hendrik Bommer and the steersman Leendert Rus, requesting on both sides most earnestly, that the action which the fiscal had against the aforementioned captain and steersman over private trade, as otherwise pretending to have, and upon which by the court of the time could not be properly inquired into according to law, might be settled by the council in a political manner, and entirely set aside. — So it is that the council has taken note here and has considered the same carefully: the above-mentioned captain and steersman together or with the others unanimously condemn in a fine of twelve hundred guilders [modern equivalent: Dutch currency], once for the benefit of the United Dutch East India Company, provided nevertheless that above this the fiscal Sir Jan van der Does shall be held to satisfy or suffice in his particular. When then further by majority of votes it is deemed good to let the same remain in their previous qualities. — Thus done and resolved in Lamtai, the suburb of Xiamen, date as above, undersigned and was signed, Pieter van Hoorn in the remaining of the qualities overruled, C. There appeared in council the fiscal Sir Joan van der Does, together with the captain Hendrik Bommer and the steersman Leendert Rus, requesting on both sides most earnestly, that the action which the fiscal had against the aforementioned captain and steersman over private trade, as otherwise pretending to have, and upon which by the court of the time could not be properly inquired into according to law, might be settled by the council in a political manner, and entirely set aside. — So it is that the council has taken note here and has considered the same carefully: the above-mentioned captain and steersman together or with the others unanimously condemn in a fine of twelve hundred guilders Dutch currency, once for the benefit of the United Dutch East India Company, provided nevertheless that above this the fiscal Sir Jan van der Does shall be held to satisfy or suffice in his particular. When then further by majority of votes it is deemed good to let the same remain in their previous qualities. — Thus done and resolved in Lamtai, the suburb of Xiamen, date as above, undersigned and was signed, Pieter van Hoorn in the remaining of the qualities overruled, C. In the evening after prayer, the lord ambassador has proposed in council that in case it should happen that the factors of the regents, after the departure, as then of the Tiger, should come to deliver some silk, whether one should send the same with the yacht the Constance over Quanzhou to Batavia, upon which it was unanimously understood to be no, since the ships in the going out and sailing of the Quanzhou strait at this time of year are subjected to too many perils, but that the Tiger should remain here until the end of this month, in hope that if there should still be time, some silk might be obtained, in order to send the same then with said fluyt to Batavia. — Furthermore, having regard to the fact that in case some silk might be obtained after the departure of the said Tiger, where one should safely preserve the same, since it is in these dwellings not without peril of fire and other inconveniences, it is unanimously understood that in case some silk should be obtained after the departure of the Tiger, that one should ship and preserve it in the yacht Bleiswijck remaining here. text_translated_detailed: October in the year 1666. Comptoir [trading post] at Nagasaki, kept by Daniel Siet, merchant and chief officer over the Company's operations in the empire of Japan. Beginning on the 18th of October in the year 1666. Monday the 18th: fair and pleasant weather with a northerly wind. In the forenoon, around 9 o'clock, I accompanied Sir Nicolaas de Rooij and the Honorable Willem Volgers to the house of the governor Kawana Gonnemon, in order to facilitate his farewell from both the city magistrates (who had gathered there according to custom). I presented to His Honor the customary compliments of thanks for all the favor, assistance, and support shown to us during this negotiation and throughout the entire year. I likewise expressed our gratitude in similar terms for such kindness, and further requested that His Honor would be pleased to take us under his protection. After the new governor Kawana Gonnemon had given me full assurance of this, we returned to the lodge. Following this, the aforementioned Honorable Volgers properly handed over to me the transport of the Company's effects remaining here at the Comptoir, amounting to ƒ 57,533: 3: 1 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], and having presented this to the people, His Honor departed toward evening with his family aboard the fluyt ship [a type of merchant vessel] the Esperance, in order to sail that same evening from this roadstead toward the Papenberg, departing with the other six ships. I was to await him there with the money and gold that still needed to be shipped. Tuesday the 19th: wind as before, but around midday the two secretaries of both city magistrates Kawana Gonnemon and Zinsabrosamma came in the name of their masters to wish me luck in my newly undertaken charge, with the recommendation that good care be taken regarding fire and light so that no accident might occur. After they had noted the names of the remaining Dutchmen as of October the 14th—the black boys (who) together with seven sailors and one bookkeeper from Correa had arrived here, making a total of 29 persons—they departed without daring to object further. Wednesday the 20th: toward evening I traveled with 56 chests of silver and the remainder of the gold to the ships lying at the Papenberg as mentioned, in order to sign and seal the papers and letters which were to be sent to various quarters. With this I was occupied the entire night and continuing until Friday the 22nd, before everything was clear and ready.

text_translated_detailed: Lacquerware that we wished to have made for the coming year. And after we had received from Bengal ninety shields and a betel box as a sample to make similar ones for 30 pieces, they asked all at once what they should charge per shield and for making the betel boxes. The price was fourteen for the shields and eight pieces per betel box. We offered them six for the shields and three guilders per betel box, but after much haggling and bidding, after we had spent well three hours with these stubborn merchants, we finally came to an agreement with them: shields at eight and the aforementioned betel boxes at four guilders each, on such conditions that these must be made according to the models of the finest lacquer, and should otherwise, if anything comes to be lacking in the quality of the lacquer, not only be unwilling to accept them at that price, but pay so much less as the quality comes to fall short. And after a written contract had previously been handed to us regarding this, they departed again. Tuesday the 16th. Fine weather with a northerly wind. Meanwhile the interpreter Josoijmon came to my chamber to write down the medicines for the Councillor Minosamma from Batavia, since that gentleman had, according to his account, written for them, which we granted him for reasons, although we placed little faith in his claim. 17th and Thursday the 18th. Wind and weather as above. This morning around 9 o'clock the interpreter Josojmon came to inform me that he had ordered the wooden boards made to lay out the gifts for the four burgomasters, namely Saquemon and Pheso, and that tomorrow their Excellencies would come to pay their respects. We trust that our interpreters will manage this work without our burden, since they will not then make any mistakes. And Tuesday the 23rd. Fine weather with steady north winds. Today our bold interpreter Josoijmon came to inform me of the reasons why the gifts to be given had not proceeded, saying that a prominent servant of the factor Saquemondonne, along with some young burghers, had severely wounded him with his sword over some affronts done to him, so that for those reasons the aforementioned gentleman was occupied. Meanwhile the governor Cauanna Gonnemond came here to the island to inspect the new gate, which had been completed some days before. And although I very kindly invited his Excellency to come to my chamber, I could not persuade him, but he put it off under the pretext of having much to do at the moment, and with that his aforementioned Excellency, after having inspected the island all around, departed again. 24th, 25th, 26th, and Saturday the 27th. These days have been rainy and very stormy weather. Nevertheless, three junks departed for Taiwan, but they did not dare to put to sea because of the rough weather but remained under the Papenberg island to await better weather.

text_translated_detailed: And on Sunday the 7th, a strong southerly wind blew. Meanwhile, five junks from Siam, Cambodia, Pattani, and Taiwan arrived here, and since we have much difficulty daily in ascertaining their cargo, and consequently often have to wait many days before we can be informed of such matters, we cannot settle such things here in Nagasaki but must conduct ourselves according to the information from the junk's logbook. On the 8th and 9th, and Wednesday the 10th, the weather has been consistently fine these days and mostly southerly winds have blown. Yesterday two Chinese junks from Pattani landed here, having brought only coarse goods to the market. Furthermore, we have been occupied today in unloading the ship the Geregtigheid [the Righteousness], during which time we received a letter from Cambodia from the Coo [uncertain: possibly a title or abbreviation] E.r. Ketting, brought here by the aforementioned Cambodian junk on the 5th of this month, reporting how on the 16th of February of this year a Chinese junk with about 600 men from Taiwan landed there, which, after they had killed well over 1,000 dishonorable Chinese pirates in the kingdom of Cambodia, took from ours 4,835 fine silver [modern equivalent: taels of silver] (under the pretext that he would have to obtain just as much from a Quang Chinese on Batavia [modern equivalent: Jakarta], they would have forcibly extorted it). Here, not being satisfied with this, the aforementioned pirate junk threatened to come and murder them all, and when they went to the ship that had come into the river to run it aground as well and let the people go that way, what will follow from these three matters, we shall learn hereafter. We nevertheless hope that God the Lord will graciously deign to preserve them from such misfortune. August in the year 1667. On the 11th and Friday the 12th, wind and weather as above. These two days nothing particular has occurred except that we have unloaded the ship the Geregtigheid of its cargo, everything coming to be properly settled with the invoice. Meanwhile, we have made known to the governor of Nagasaki the improper procedures committed by the Taiwanese Chinese against ours in Cambodia, who thereupon had the Chinese from the junks come from Cambodia sharply examined and interrogated, and found the matter in substance mostly as we had reported to him from the letter of C.r. Ketting. On the 13th and Sunday the 14th, continuation of fine and pleasant weather with southerly wind. Today the governor of Nagasaki has had all the hides from the sorting brought to his house. In order to have three or four hundred of the best selected for the emperor, and after they had selected about 12 or 13 hundred of the most suitable ones, these were properly sealed and brought back to the island with the others. When the trade begins, from those 12 or 13 hundred three hundred of the best will be selected and then paid for at the price that the others will come to be worth. Monday the 15th, still steadily fine and pleasant weather being present. We received today through a messenger from Fukuoka news that a ship was seen at sea about 15 Japanese miles far outside the coast, but since it was calm and evening was approaching, we did not think it good that anyone should sail out to investigate it. Meanwhile, we understood from the mouth of our interpreters how a certain stokoseemon, a prominent merchant and factor of the honored lord of Faccata, having been called today before his lord (who had come here to Nagasaki for that purpose), and being accused of being one of that college which had traded on Correa, the aforementioned stokoseemon firmly and strongly denied this. And in order to convince him of it, his secretary was called, who presumed well what was going on, said it would follow immediately, and went straight inside as if he were going to change clothes, where the same man thereupon, without further deliberation, cut his belly open with a cross, because he did not want to be forced by torture to betray or reveal his lord, especially since he himself was guilty of it. On the 16th, 17th, and Thursday the 18th, it has been uncommonly calm so that the ship which was seen on the 15th of this month has approached the coast little or not at all. Today the governor of Nagasaki has had a cattij of massoij brought to be divided among 2 or 3 druggists, who will investigate what medicinal properties are hidden in it. Friday the 19th, weather and wind as above being present, we received a little before midday with a messenger which had been sent out expressly for that purpose, news that the ship which was seen on the 15th of this month was close under the coast. We would, after we had taken the midday meal, send the merchant E.r. de Rooij out for that purpose, who, returning, reported that it was the yacht the Schelvis [the Flounder] from Cambodia, and from the mouth of the arriving friends we understood with sorrow how the Chinese in Cambodia, the Company's lodge on the 10th of July, about midday, after the aforementioned ship had lain near the lodge for about a day, had shamefully murdered the chief Pieter Ketting with three more black youths. The remaining people, having saved themselves by flight to the yacht the Schelvis, the Company's goods were for the most part and all the rice warehouses plundered by the aforementioned Chinese. Furthermore, the Company's dwellings there were burned to the ground. Three Dutchmen by the names of Jurriaan Rouw, formerly a sea gunner, Pieter Sijmonsen, a fisherman from Den Helder, a sailor, and Daniel Verdonck from Groningen from Zealand, were that evening before the lodge was attacked with the aforementioned lodge. Also all the books, both of the Chinese trade as well as the lodge, were burned. Thus we cannot be given a proper account of what damage the Company suffers thereby.

text_translated_detailed: Memorandum for the Honorable Constantinus Ranst to serve his Honor as guidance, given by the Merchant Daniel Six upon his departure to Batavia. How your Honor shall conduct yourself toward the Iedose court journey [a journey to the court of the Shogun in Edo] on the way itself in Jedo [Edo], and upon returning, shall have to conduct yourself (besides that your Honor through experience has sufficiently learned this already) is indicated in the abundant subsequent daily notes and examined writings left behind by our forefathers, by which, because nothing particularly or noteworthy new has occurred during my presence here, I do not know to add, the less so since we must be entirely subject to the manner and pleasure of the Nagasaki governors (who shall henceforth concern themselves alone with the Company's affairs). This I advise your Honor (so far as your Honor's wise judgment and experience shall be able to find good to follow for the least offense to our nation). Regarding the gifts to be given at court as well as to the Burgomaster and others of Nagasaki, your Honor is best suited for this, left over from what has come this year. You need not provide new council lords with gifts, but if, contrary to our expectation, any new councilors were appointed by the emperor, your Honor is provided for this in abundance, indeed you shall even have gifts left over. At court, the gifts we gave last year on the recommendation of your Honor's followers and with the approval of the Merchant Mister de Rooij, in the presence of the governor of Nagasaki, such gifts may be accepted, approximately budgeted at sixteen hundred guilders [modern equivalent: approximately 16,000 euros in modern currency], both for the emperor as well as the imperial councilors. Whether your Honor with us shall enter upon this path, we shall leave to your Honor's wise judgment and good deliberation. As for myself, if it should again fall to me to do it, in order to make the Company as agreeable as possible at court, I would let the 2 horses which were sent from Batavia for that purpose serve as an extraordinary gift in addition, but

The third Tongjin Tonginse junk has not appeared here this year, such that it must have returned to Kongjin bouqun without accomplishing its purpose or landed elsewhere.
